problems.title: Build a Matrix With Conditions
problems.primitivesUsed: Algorithms.TopologicalSort.TopologicalSort.TrySort, run once over rowConditions and once over colConditions (two fresh ValueNode/ValueTopology graphs, mirroring CourseSchedule/Fixtures' CourseNode/CourseTopology shape) to get each value's row index and column index directly from each ordering's position; TrySort's own false-on-cycle result is exactly LeetCode's 'return an empty matrix' signal, so no separate cycle check was needed.
problems.notes: 3 xUnit cases pass: the official LC example (assertions check the general before/after row and column relations rather than one fixed matrix, since any valid placement is accepted), a genuine 3-node row cycle returning an empty matrix, and a no-conditions case placing every value exactly once. Benchmark compares a naive O(V^2+VE) rescan-based toposort against Kahn's TopologicalSort.TrySort, each run twice per invocation (row axis + column axis) at K=50/1000, mirroring CourseScheduleIIBenchmarks' contrast. A temporary smoke-test console app (built solely for this verification, deleted after use) confirmed both benchmark methods return identical combined ordering counts at both sizes. Full test suite: 2783 passed, 1 pre-existing skip, 0 failed.

problems.title: Maximum Number of Robots Within Budget
problems.primitivesUsed: DataStructures.Deque.Deque<int> as a monotonic decreasing-chargeTimes index window (SlidingWindowMaximumTests precedent) for the window-max term of cost = max(chargeTimes)+k*sum(runningCosts), plus a running long sum for the running-cost term; two-pointer window shrinks from the left whenever cost exceeds budget.
problems.notes: Verified against both official LC examples (answers 3 and 0) by hand-tracing the algorithm before coding. Benchmark: O(n) rescan-per-left baseline vs. O(n) total monotonic-deque sliding window. All 3 tests pass; cross-checked baseline vs. deque agree via a standalone harness at Length=20/500; full suite 2783/2784 (1 pre-existing skip).

problems.title: Number of Ways to Reach a Position After Exactly k Steps
problems.primitivesUsed: Algorithms.DynamicProgramming.Memoizer<TState,TResult> (TargetSumTests / NumberOfWaysToRearrangeSticksWithKSticksVisibleTests precedent) - top-down (remainingSteps, distanceToTarget) recurrence over the collapsed absolute-distance state, mod 1e9+7.
problems.notes: Verified against both official LC examples (3 and 0) plus a k=0 base case, and independently cross-checked K=18 against the closed-form C(18,10)=43758 via a standalone harness. Benchmark: exponential un-memoized recursion vs. Memoizer-cached (TargetSumBenchmarks' shape), K kept modest (18,22). All 3 tests pass; full suite 2783/2784 (1 pre-existing skip).

problems.title: Meeting Rooms III
problems.primitivesUsed: DataStructures.Heap.Heap<Element,TOrder> used twice (FindServersThatHandledMostNumberOfRequestsTests' two-structure precedent): Heap<int, MinHeapOrder<int>> as the free-room pool (root = lowest free room) and Heap<(long End, int Room), MinHeapOrder<(long,int)>> as the busy-room pool ordered by end time then room number via ValueTuple's own IComparable.
problems.notes: Room-assignment simulation hand-verified against both official LC examples (n=2 -> room 0, n=3 -> room 1, both tie-break cases) before coding. Benchmark: O(RoomCount) linear freeAt[] scan per meeting vs. O(log RoomCount) two-heap pool, adapting FindServersThatHandledMostNumberOfRequestsBenchmarks' ring-of-servers shape to a fixed room pool. All 3 tests pass; cross-checked baseline vs. two-heap agree via a standalone harness at RoomCount=5/20; full suite 2783/2784 (1 pre-existing skip).

problems.title: Longest Increasing Subsequence II
problems.primitivesUsed: SegmentTree<int,MaxOperation<int>> keyed directly by value (dp[v] = LIS length ending at value v; Query(num-k,num-1) for best predecessor, Update(num,·) to record it) - same instantiation BookingConcertTicketsInGroupsTests already uses.
problems.notes: Manually hand-simulated both LeetCode examples against the sweep before trusting the xUnit run (both matched). Benchmark: O(n^2) DP baseline vs O(n log maxValue) segment-tree sweep. Build clean, 3/3 tests pass.

problems.title: Design SQL
problems.primitivesUsed: HashMap<TKey,TValue> nested two levels (HashMap<string,Table>, each Table a HashMap<int,string[]> keyed by an ever-increasing row id) - same HashMap-of-HashMap composition style as DesignMovieRentalSystemTests.
problems.notes: Benchmark: List<(int,string[])> linear-scan table vs HashMap<int,string[]> table, same shape as DesignANumberContainerSystemBenchmarks. Build clean, 3/3 tests pass.

problems.title: Sum of Prefix Scores of Strings
problems.primitivesUsed: LowercaseTrie<int>, walked via its public Root/Children (same navigation MapSumPairsBenchmarks.WalkTo uses) - increment each node's Value while inserting each word (instead of only the end-of-word node) so Value counts words sharing that prefix; scoring sums counts along a word's own path.
problems.notes: Manually hand-traced both LeetCode examples through the trie before trusting the xUnit run (both matched). Benchmark: O(wordCount^2*wordLength) StartsWith rescan vs O(wordCount*wordLength) prefix-counting trie. Build clean, 3/3 tests pass.

problems.title: Number of Good Paths
problems.primitivesUsed: DataStructures/DisjointSet/DisjointSet.cs (Union-Find): edges sorted by higher-valued endpoint, unioned in increasing order while tracking each component's max value and count-at-max as side state to count newly-formed same-value pairs on each merge.

problems.title: Longest Uploaded Prefix
problems.primitivesUsed: DataStructures/Set/Set.cs (HashMap-backed membership set): tracks uploaded video numbers; a monotonic frontier pointer advances past every already-uploaded value, O(1) amortized per Upload.

problems.title: Number of Pairs Satisfying Inequality
problems.primitivesUsed: DataStructures/FenwickTree/FenwickTree.cs (SumOperation<int> BIT) + Algorithms/Searching/BinarySearch.cs (UpperBound/LowerBound) + DataStructures/Sequence/ArraySequence.cs: coordinate-compressed diff[i]=nums1[i]-nums2[i], left-to-right sweep counting diff[i] <= diff[j]+diff via prefix counts, same pattern as the existing CountOfSmallerNumbersAfterSelf coverage.

problems.title: Number of Common Factors
problems.primitivesUsed: DataStructures/Set/Set.cs (HashMap-backed Set<int>): every common factor of a and b is a divisor of gcd(a,b) (gcd computed with plain Euclid's-algorithm arithmetic, no primitive needed), so divisors are enumerated only up to sqrt(gcd) and the two divisors found per step (i and gcd/i) are deduplicated through Set<int> for the i*i==gcd boundary case - the same dedupe-by-membership role CountLatticePointsInsideACircleTests already established for its own Set<(int,int)>. Benchmark compares the O(min(a,b)) linear scan baseline against the sqrt(gcd) Set-based enumeration.

problems.title: Maximum Deletions on a String
problems.primitivesUsed: DataStructures/RollingHash/RollingHash.cs: dp[i] = 1 + best dp[i+k] over every half-length k in [1,(n-i)/2] where s[i..i+k)==s[i+k..i+2k) (or 1 alone if none exist), with each candidate equality checked via RollingHash's O(1) hash screen followed by a real SequenceEqual verify - the exact screen-then-verify composition DistinctEchoSubstringsTests already established, applied per DP transition here instead of per dedup candidate. All 4 test cases were hand-simulated (not copied from a possibly-misremembered LeetCode example) to confirm the 'take the max over every valid k, not just the smallest' recurrence, e.g. 'aaabaab' needs the larger k=3 deletion before the smaller k=1 ones to reach the true maximum of 4 operations. Benchmark compares an allocation-heavy .Substring+== baseline DP against the RollingHash-screened span-based DP.

problems.title: Count Subarrays With Fixed Bounds
problems.primitivesUsed: DataStructures/SegmentTree/SegmentTree.cs with MinOperation<int> and MaxOperation<int>: a subarray qualifies iff its SegmentTree-queried min equals minK and max equals maxK (which, since min==minK forces every element >=minK and max==maxK forces every element <=maxK, is already sufficient - no separate range check needed), the same Min/Max SegmentTree pairing BookingConcertTicketsInGroupsTests already uses. Benchmark compares a triple-nested-loop baseline that rescans each subarray from scratch against the SegmentTree O(log n)-per-query version.

problems.title: Words Within Two Edits of Dictionary
problems.primitivesUsed: DataStructures.Graph.Engines.Dags.Trees.LowercaseTrie<bool> - dictionary words are Set into it, then each query walks it via a budgeted DFS over the trie's own Root/Children (the same navigation ImplementMagicDictionaryTests.Search already rehearses), generalized from an exactly-one-substitution budget to an at-most-two-edits budget.
problems.notes: Benchmark compares brute force (scan every dictionary word, count mismatched characters with early exit at >2) against the LowercaseTrie budgeted-DFS search. Dry-run smoke test (DictionarySize=2000/6000, WordLength=8) showed TrieSearch actually slower than BruteForce here (100ms vs 32ms at 2000; 302ms vs 179ms at 6000, 17-19x more allocation) - the budget-2 DFS's 26-way branching at every mismatched position does genuinely more work than a tight linear compare-and-early-exit loop at this word length/dictionary size; a real trade-off, not a bug. All 3 new tests pass; both projects build clean in Debug/Release; benchmark dry-run completed with no exceptions.

problems.title: Next Greater Element IV
problems.primitivesUsed: DataStructures.Stack.Stack<int> x3 (waitingForFirst/waitingForSecond/promoted) - the classic two-monotonic-stack sweep, same Stack<int> precedent as NextGreaterElementIITests, generalized from 'first greater' to 'second greater' by routing waitingForFirst's resolved indices through a small promoted stack into waitingForSecond instead of resolving them outright.
problems.notes: Benchmark compares O(n^2) brute force (scan forward counting values greater than nums[i] until the 2nd shows up) against the O(n) two-stack sweep. Dry-run smoke test (Length=200/5000, values in [1,999]) showed BruteForce winning in wall-clock at these sizes/value-range - matches the already-established NextGreaterElementIIBenchmarks precedent exactly, which shows the identical pattern for the same reason (pigeonhole bounds the average brute-force inner-loop scan length well below n, while three Stack<T> instances add real per-op constant overhead); not a regression. Caught and fixed one wrong hand-computed expected value during the test run: for a strictly-increasing array, 'second greater' need not exceed the first greater value, just nums[i] itself, so [1,2,3,4] -> [3,4,-1,-1], not all -1. All 4 new tests pass; both projects build clean in Debug/Release; benchmark dry-run completed with no exceptions.

problems.title: Closest Nodes Queries in a Binary Search Tree
problems.primitivesUsed: DataStructures.Graph.Engines.Dags.Trees.InOrderTraversal.Walk/IInOrderHooks<int> (same AsyncLocal-state hook idiom as FindModeInBinarySearchTreeTests/KthSmallestElementInABSTTests) collecting sorted node values into DataStructures.DynamicArray.DynamicArray<int>, then Algorithms.Searching.BinarySearch.LowerBound over DataStructures.Sequence.DynamicArraySequence<int> for floor/ceiling per query - the same insertion-point-to-floor/ceiling move ClosestRoomTests already proves out, generalized to report both neighbors instead of picking whichever is nearer. Benchmark fixture also uses BinarySearchTree<int>.Insert/.Root to build the tree.
problems.notes: Benchmark compares an O(n) per-query recursive full-tree scan (ignoring BST order entirely) against O(n) one-time in-order collection plus O(log n) BinarySearch.LowerBound per query. Dry-run smoke test (NodeCount=500/20000) showed the expected dramatic gap: 2.84s vs 7.2ms at NodeCount=20000 (~390x). All 2 new tests pass; both projects build clean in Debug/Release; benchmark dry-run completed with no exceptions.

problems.title: Minimum Cuts to Divide a Circle
problems.primitivesUsed: Plain arithmetic parity check (n==1?0:n%2==0?n/2:n) - lighter repo-primitive fit, same shape as PowerOfTwoTests.cs/NumberOf1BitsTests.cs. No existing DSA primitive genuinely composes here: the correct recurrence is a closed-form parity fact (diameter cuts only pair opposite slices when n is even), not a search/DP structure - I verified a naive 'remaining-parity' DP framing gives a WRONG answer for odd n, so Memoizer was deliberately not forced in.
problems.notes: Benchmark compares an O(n) unrolled cut-by-cut simulation against the O(1) closed form; dry-run smoke test showed the expected growing gap (SimulateOneCutAtATime 244us->423us across Slices=101->100001, ClosedFormParityCheck flat at ~203us).

problems.title: Remove Nodes From Linked List
problems.primitivesUsed: DataStructures.Stack.Stack<SinglyLinkedListNode<int>> composed with DataStructures.SinglyLinkedList.SinglyLinkedListNode<int> - monotonic non-increasing stack sweep (same shape as AsteroidCollisionTests.cs/DailyTemperaturesTests.cs/NextGreaterNodeInLinkedListTests.cs), popping nodes made obsolete by a later greater value, then relinking survivors.
problems.notes: Benchmark compares O(n^2) brute-force right-scan vs O(n) monotonic stack sweep; both dry-run smoke-tested successfully at Length=200/5000.

problems.title: Minimum Score of a Path Between Two Cities
problems.primitivesUsed: DataStructures.DisjointSet.DisjointSet - unions every road's endpoints, then reduces to the min weight among roads whose endpoint root matches city 1's root (a path can revisit edges freely, so the answer is the min edge weight anywhere in city 1's connected component); same Union-Find-for-component-membership move as GraphConnectivityWithThresholdTests.cs/NumberOfProvincesTests.cs.
problems.notes: Benchmark compares a BFS flood-fill baseline vs DisjointSet union-find; both dry-run smoke-tested successfully at CityCount=200/5000. Full xUnit suite (2813 passed, 1 pre-existing skip) and Release builds (0 warnings) verified for all three problems together after all six files were added; manifest.json entries for ids 2481/2487/2492 updated to status 'done' with these paths.

problems.title: Divide Nodes Into the Maximum Number of Groups
problems.primitivesUsed: Algorithms.Bipartiteness.BipartiteCheck.IsBipartite (multi-root 2-coloring, returns -1 case) + DataStructures.KeyedDisjointSet<int> (component grouping via union over the edge list, same shape FindAllPeopleWithSecretTests uses) + Algorithms.Reducing.Reduce.Graph with BreadthFirstReduceOrder<TNode> and DistanceMapReduceAlgebra<TNode> (per-root BFS distance map, same composition WordLadderTests/MinimumGeneticMutationTests use, read here for its max value = eccentricity instead of one target's distance, tried once per node). Node/topology fixtures (GroupNode/GroupTopology) follow the PossibleBipartitionTests/MinimumGeneticMutationTests Fixtures/ pattern.
problems.notes: 3 tests (LeetCode's two published examples plus a custom two-disjoint-bipartite-components case proving the per-component summing, not just a single BFS root over the whole graph) all pass. Benchmark compares a hand-rolled array-adjacency baseline (Queue<int> BFS coloring, int[] union-find, int[] distance-array BFS) against the repo-primitive composition over a random spanning tree (connected + bipartite by construction, forcing every node's full BFS). A ShortRun dry run showed the primitive composition genuinely correct (cross-validated bit-for-bit against the baseline across NodeCount=2..60 via a temporary verification harness, reverted afterward) but ~11-13x slower and far more allocation-heavy than the raw-array version, driven by a fresh Dictionary<TNode,int> + HashSet-backed TrackedVisitGuard per BFS root call (V calls total) - documented honestly in the benchmark's header comment (same 'correct composition, not always a win' precedent MatrixCellsInDistanceOrderBenchmarks already sets) rather than reframed to look favorable.

problems.title: Delete Greatest Value in Each Row
problems.primitivesUsed: Algorithms.Sorting.MergeSort.Sort<int,ArrayIndexedSequence<int>> (sort each row ascending), same composition ArrayPartitionTests already uses - once every row is sorted, the values deleted together on round j are exactly column j, so the answer is the sum of each column's max.
problems.notes: 2 tests (both LeetCode published examples) pass. Benchmark compares the problem's own repeated-simulation baseline (O(Rows*Columns^2): find-and-remove each row's current max, Columns times) against MergeSort-per-row + single column-max pass (O(Rows*Columns*log Columns)); cross-validated equal outputs against the baseline for Columns=1..30 via the same temporary harness used for the other two problems in this cluster.

problems.title: Design Memory Allocator
problems.primitivesUsed: DataStructures.HashMap.HashMap<int, DynamicArray<int>> (mID -> currently-owned memory indices) composed with DataStructures.DynamicArray.DynamicArray<int>, alongside a plain int[] memory array (0 = free) for the leftmost-free-run scan Allocate needs - the same 'raw array + HashMap index' shape DesignANumberContainerSystemTests' own NumberContainers already uses, here tracking a set of indices per key instead of one.
problems.notes: 2 tests pass (LeetCode's full published call/output trace, plus a no-room-left case). Benchmark holds Allocate identical between both [Benchmark] methods (it is not the axis under test) and compares Free strategies: ArrayScanFree rescans the whole memory array per call vs. HashMapTrackedFree visiting only the tracked indices. A ShortRun dry run showed HashMapTrackedFree genuinely faster (~0.71x at Count=200, ~0.46x at Count=2000) despite extra allocation overhead, and outputs were cross-validated identical against the baseline for Count=1..50 via a temporary verification harness added to Program.cs and reverted afterward (git diff confirmed clean before/after).

problems.title: Maximum Number of Points From Grid Queries
problems.primitivesUsed: DataStructures.Heap.Heap<Element,TOrder> closed over DataStructures.Graph.ShortestPaths.ByPriorityOrder<GridNode,int> as a min-heap over cell value (same frontier shape ShortestPath.Dijkstra uses), composed with Graph.Grids' GridNode/GridChildren/GridTopology for 4-directional neighbor arithmetic over an all-passable Grid, plus a HashSet<GridNode> for visited-tracking.
problems.notes: Optimal play only ever steps onto cells below the query threshold, so each query's answer is the size of the below-threshold connected region reachable from (0,0); sorting queries ascending and draining one shared min-heap flood fill answers all of them in a single pass. 3 hand-traced xUnit cases pass. Benchmark: per-query from-scratch DFS flood fill vs. the shared min-heap flood fill on a fixed 60x60 grid, QueriesCount in {50,1000}. Cross-validated the algorithm against an independent PriorityQueue-based reference across 500 randomized grids (temporary scratch harness, zero mismatches). Full suite 2876 passed / 1 pre-existing skip; both projects build Release with 0 warnings.

problems.title: Smallest Value After Replacing With Sum of Prime Factors
problems.notes: Core step is trial-division prime factorization (sum of prime factors with multiplicity, repeated to a fixed point) - pure number theory with no existing primitive to compose. Searched DataStructures/** and Algorithms/** for Prime/Sieve/Factor/IsPrime/GCD; only unrelated hits (AlgorithmConstants.BranchingFactor, RoomWaysPrecomputedFactorialAlgebra's factorials, HashMapStorage's growth factor). No Sieve of Eratosthenes / trial-division / any number-theory primitive exists to compose - writing one from scratch here would be inventing a new production primitive, which this task disallows. A genuine Algorithms/NumberTheory PrimeFactorization or Sieve primitive would need to land first.

problems.title: Cycle Length Queries in a Tree
problems.primitivesUsed: DataStructures.Heap.HeapArrayIndex.Parent - node ids 1..2^n-1 pack a complete binary tree the same way Heap's own backing array does (parent(id)=id/2, children 2*id/2*id+1); shifting each id down by one (index=id-1) makes the library's existing 0-indexed Parent arithmetic exactly equivalent to the problem's 1-indexed walk (verified algebraically and by cross-check). No tree is ever materialized.
problems.notes: Cycle length = 1 + tree-distance(a,b), computed by walking the deeper node up then both up together to the LCA, driven by HeapArrayIndex.Parent. 2 xUnit cases pass (LeetCode's published n=3 example, hand-verified, plus a hand-traced n=2 case). Benchmark: per-query Dictionary<int,int>-allocating ancestor walk vs. zero-allocation Parent-arithmetic two-pointer walk at QueriesCount in {1000,20000} - both O(log id) per query, so this demonstrates an allocation gap via MemoryDiagnoser rather than Big-O. Cross-validated against a from-scratch materialized-adjacency-list BFS ground truth across 2000 randomized trials (temporary scratch harness, zero mismatches). Full suite 2876 passed / 1 pre-existing skip; both projects build Release with 0 warnings.

problems.title: Minimize the Maximum of Two Arrays
problems.primitivesUsed: Algorithms.Searching.BinarySearch.LowerBound over a new IRandomAccessSequence<bool> witness (FeasibleMaximumSequence) implementing the standard binary-search-on-the-answer + inclusion-exclusion feasibility check (eligible1/eligible2/eligibleEither via lcm(divisor1,divisor2)), same shape as the existing KokoEatingBananas/SplitArrayLargestSum coverage.
problems.notes: 3/3 tests pass against hand-verified LeetCode examples (2,7,1,3)->4, (3,5,2,1)->3, (2,4,8,2)->15. Benchmark: hand-rolled bisection vs BinarySearch.LowerBound, Params UniqueCountScale=1_000/1_000_000, dry-run smoke test clean. Full test suite: 2903 passed, 0 failed, 1 pre-existing skip.

problems.title: Count Anagrams
problems.primitivesUsed: Domain.Modular.ModularArithmetic (Modulo=1e9+7, Fermat's-little-theorem Inverse) driving a precomputed factorial/inverse-factorial table, the same shape LeetCode/CountWaysToBuildRoomsInAnAntColony/RoomWaysPrecomputedFactorialAlgebra already uses. New CountAnagramsSolution.cs (DSAExperimentation/LeetCode/CountAnagrams, TwoSumSolution-shaped) computes each word's multinomial-coefficient distinct-permutation count and multiplies mod 1e9+7, plus a brute-force permutation-enumeration baseline.
problems.notes: 10/10 tests pass (5 examples x 2 strategies; 'too hot'->18 and 'aa'->1 are official LeetCode examples, 'a'->1/'banana'->60/'ab ba'->4 hand-verified). Benchmark: HashSet-deduped recursive permutation enumeration vs modular factorial table, Params WordLength=4/7, dry-run smoke test shows expected divergence (brute force allocates and scales factorially; modular stays flat, zero allocation). Full test suite: 2903 passed, 0 failed, 1 pre-existing skip.

problems.title: Shortest Distance to Target String in a Circular Array
problems.primitivesUsed: Algorithms.Reducing.Reduce.Graph + DistanceMapReduceAlgebra<TNode> (unmodified) running BFS from startIndex over a new IGraphTopology witness (CircularArrayNode/CircularArrayTopology) whose two edges per node are the circular (index-1+n)%n and (index+1)%n steps - same composition SmallestIntegerDivisibleByK coverage already uses, just over a 2-neighbor circular graph. Answer is the min BFS distance over nodes whose word equals target.
problems.notes: 3/3 tests pass against LeetCode's own 3 examples. Fixtures/ subfolder added (custom node+topology types, CourseSchedule precedent) and duplicated into DSAExperimentation.Benchmarks/Fixtures (CircularArrayNode/Topology/Graphs, RemainderNode/Graphs precedent) since Benchmarks doesn't reference Tests. Benchmark: direct min(diff,n-diff) linear scan vs Reduce.Graph BFS, Params Length=200/5_000, target diametrically opposite startIndex, dry-run smoke test clean. Full test suite: 2903 passed, 0 failed, 1 pre-existing skip.

problems.title: Distinct Prime Factors of Product of Array
problems.primitivesUsed: DSAExperimentation.DataStructures.Set.Set<int> (HashMap-backed) for dedup, fed by per-element trial-division prime factorization (harness logic, same shape as LargestComponentSizeByCommonFactorTests' PrimeFactors + NumberOfCommonFactorsTests' Set<int> composition). The product's prime factors are exactly the union of each element's own factors, so the product itself is never formed.
problems.notes: 3 xUnit theory cases pass. Benchmark baseline actually forms the BigInteger product (O(n^2)-shaped blowup, same family as AddTwoNumbersBenchmarks' BigInteger arm) then trial-divides it, vs. per-element trial division into Set<int>. Both Tests and Benchmarks projects build 0 warnings/errors (Release); full LeetCodeCoverage suite (2284 tests) passes.

problems.title: Closest Prime Numbers in Range
problems.primitivesUsed: DSAExperimentation.DataStructures.DynamicArray.DynamicArray<bool> as the Sieve of Eratosthenes composite-tracking array, the exact composition CountPrimesTests already established for LC 204, run once up to `right` then scanned for the smallest gap between consecutive primes in [left, right].
problems.notes: 3 xUnit theory cases (both LeetCode examples plus a minimal twin-prime range) pass. Benchmark mirrors CountPrimesBenchmarks' shape: trial-division scan vs. DynamicArray<bool> sieve. Both projects build 0 warnings/errors (Release); full LeetCodeCoverage suite (2284 tests) passes.

problems.title: Find Consecutive Integers from a Data Stream
problems.primitivesUsed: DSAExperimentation.DataStructures.Deque.Deque<int> holding a fixed-size window of the last k values (PushBack/TryPopFront), the same windowing shape SlidingWindowMaximumTests uses, with a match count against `value` maintained incrementally as the window slides.
problems.notes: 3 xUnit facts pass (official LC call trace, fewer-than-k case, mismatch-then-refill case). Benchmark compares an unbounded-history List<int> rescanned per call (O(n*k)) vs. the Deque<int>-windowed incremental count (O(n)). Both projects build 0 warnings/errors (Release); full LeetCodeCoverage suite (2284 tests) passes. No Workflow tool was available in this environment (the leetcode-coverage skill's invocation instructions named a Workflow tool that isn't registered here), so this cluster's Select/Implement/Verify/Record phases were carried out directly rather than via that script; manifest.json was updated by hand for these three ids only.

problems.title: Maximize the Minimum Powered City
problems.primitivesUsed: Algorithms/Searching/BinarySearch.LowerBound over an on-demand DataStructures/Sequence/IRandomAccessSequence<bool> 'infeasible target' sequence for the binary-search-on-the-answer (the same InfeasibleSequence + LowerBound(seq,true)-1 'maximize the answer' shape MaximumNumberOfTasksYouCanAssignTests already established), plus DataStructures/RangeFenwickTree/RangeFenwickTree<long,ScaledSumOperation<long>> for the greedy per-target feasibility check (RangeAdd for both each station's initial coverage and each greedy top-up, Query(i,i) for the point read - exactly RangeFenwickTree's documented range-update/point-query purpose). Benchmark contrasts a descending LinearScan over every candidate target vs. SequenceLowerBound, both sharing the identical RangeFenwickTree-backed Feasible check, mirroring MaximumNumberOfTasksYouCanAssignBenchmarks/KokoEatingBananasBenchmarks. Verified: dotnet build (Debug, Tests) and dotnet test (11/11 passing incl. this problem's 3 test cases) + dotnet build (Release, Benchmarks) both succeeded.

problems.title: Check if Point Is Reachable
problems.primitivesUsed: Test: the analytic solution (gcd(targetX,targetY) is a power of two) uses only a private Euclidean Gcd helper plus the n&(n-1)==0 bit trick - no repo DataStructures/Algorithms primitive applies to that piece, the same judgment call FindGreatestCommonDivisorOfArrayTests/CheckIfItIsAGoodArrayTests/XOfAKindInADeckOfCardsTests already made and left inline rather than promoting. Benchmark composes real repo primitives for its brute-force baseline: DataStructures/Queue/Queue<Element> + DataStructures/Set/Set<Element> running a BFS over the four reachability moves (bounded by target coordinates), contrasted against the analytic Gcd check - mirroring WordLadderSolution's 'textbook Queue+Set BFS' precedent and TwoSumBenchmarks' brute-force-vs-closed-form shape. Verified: dotnet build (Debug, Tests) and dotnet test (11/11 passing incl. this problem's 5 test cases) + dotnet build (Release, Benchmarks) both succeeded (required aliasing DataStructures.Queue.Queue<T> as RepoQueue to resolve the CS0104 ambiguity against System.Collections.Generic.Queue<T>, the same alias trick RepoDeque already uses elsewhere in this repo).

problems.title: Count Collisions of Monkeys on a Polygon
problems.primitivesUsed: No DataStructures/Algorithms primitive applies - the answer is the closed form (2^n - 2) mod 1e9+7, computed via a private ModPow (exponentiation by squaring) helper, the same 'no repo container or algorithm primitive applies here' judgment call this repo already makes for small numeric primitives (FindGreatestCommonDivisorOfArrayTests' Euclidean Gcd precedent). Benchmark runs the same 'two ways to compute the same fold' contrast FindGreatestCommonDivisorOfArrayBenchmarks already uses: naive O(n) repeated-multiplication vs. O(log n) exponentiation-by-squaring. Verified: dotnet build (Debug, Tests) and dotnet test (11/11 passing incl. this problem's 3 test cases) + dotnet build (Release, Benchmarks) both succeeded.

problems.title: Count Increasing Quadruplets
problems.primitivesUsed: FenwickTree<int,SumOperation<int>> from DataStructures/FenwickTree (Binary Indexed Tree of counts) as a suffix 'count values greater than X' structure, swept right-to-left over k; a plain running int counter (no data structure needed) tracks the left-side 'count values less than nums[k] before position j' factor since that threshold is fixed for the whole inner j-loop. O(n^2 log n). Verified against both LeetCode examples by hand before coding, and via dotnet test.
problems.notes: Verified: dotnet build (Debug, Tests project) and dotnet test (Theory over both LeetCode examples + 1 extra strictly-decreasing edge case, all passing) + dotnet build (Release, Benchmarks project) succeeded, 0 warnings/errors.

problems.title: House Robber IV

problems.notes: Verified: dotnet build (Debug, Tests) and dotnet test (both LeetCode examples + 1 k-equals-house-count edge case, all passing) + dotnet build (Release, Benchmarks) succeeded, 0 warnings/errors.

problems.title: Handling Sum Queries After Update
problems.primitivesUsed: LazySegmentTree<int,bool,TOperation> from DataStructures/LazySegmentTree, generalized via a new IRangeUpdateOperation<int,bool> witness (FlipCountOperation: ApplyUpdate flips a range's one-count to rangeLength-count, ComposeUpdate XORs pending flips) tracking count-of-ones under range flip; a running long sum is incremented by p*ones per type-2 query. Same 'compose the generic lazy-propagation engine over a new algebra' move FancySequenceTests' AffineOperation already makes.
problems.notes: Verified: dotnet build (Debug, Tests) and dotnet test (both LeetCode examples + 1 cancelling-double-flip edge case, all passing) + dotnet build (Release, Benchmarks) succeeded, 0 warnings/errors.

problems.title: Count the Number of Square-Free Subsets
problems.primitivesUsed: Algorithms/DynamicProgramming/Memoizer.cs (memoized bitmask-state recurrence over the 10 primes <= 30) + Domain/Modular/ModularArithmetic.cs (mod 1e9+7, and Power for 2^ones). Solution lives at DSAExperimentation/LeetCode/CountTheNumberOfSquareFreeSubsets/CountTheNumberOfSquareFreeSubsetsSolution.cs (CountByBruteForce baseline: O(2^n) subset enumeration; CountByBitmaskMemo: Memoizer-driven bitmask DP). Build + all 20 new xUnit tests pass (dotnet test); BenchmarkDotNet dry-run of both [Benchmark] arms (Length=15,20) completes cleanly.

problems.title: Find the String with LCP
problems.primitivesUsed: DataStructures/DisjointSet/{DisjointSet,DisjointSetForest}.cs (Union-Find over 'same character' as an equivalence relation on positions). Solution lives at DSAExperimentation/LeetCode/FindTheStringWithLCP/FindTheStringWithLCPSolution.cs (ConstructByDirectSweep baseline: textbook nested-loop grouping; ConstructByDisjointSet: DisjointSet-based grouping); both arms share a private IsConsistent reconstruction/validation step (required by the problem to reject unrealizable lcp matrices). Build + all tests pass; BenchmarkDotNet dry-run (Length=50,300, random string over a 4-letter alphabet so Union does real merging) completes cleanly.

problems.title: Minimum Time to Visit a Cell In a Grid
problems.primitivesUsed: DataStructures/Heap/Heap.cs + DataStructures/Graph/ShortestPaths/ByPriorityOrder.cs, composed directly (the same frontier ShortestPath.Dijkstra/AStar and MinimumCostToMakeAtLeastOneValidPathInAGridTests already use). The generic ShortestPath.Dijkstra/GridShortestPath engines were NOT usable as-is because this problem's per-edge cost (the 'wait for parity' formula) is a function of the caller's current best distance, not a static per-edge weight their IEdgeTopology/BFS-distance APIs assume - so the relaxation loop itself is composed directly in the Solution tier over the existing Heap primitive, not a modification to Algorithms/ShortestPaths. Solution lives at DSAExperimentation/LeetCode/MinimumTimeToVisitACellInAGrid/MinimumTimeToVisitACellInAGridSolution.cs (MinimumTimeByBclPriorityQueue baseline: identical algorithm fronted by BCL PriorityQueue<T,TPriority>; MinimumTimeByHeap: composed, fronted by this repo's Heap<Element,TOrder>). Build + all tests pass (LeetCode's own 2 published examples plus a 1x1 trivial case); BenchmarkDotNet dry-run (Size=20,60) completes cleanly.

problems.title: Split the Array to Make Coprime Products
problems.primitivesUsed: DataStructures.HashMap<int,int> tracking each prime factor's rightmost index (same map-a-key-to-latest-index shape as LargestComponentSizeByCommonFactorTests), swept left-to-right with a running boundary; prime factorization is local plain-algorithm glue, precedented by that same test file's own local PrimeFactors helper. Benchmark baseline is a BigInteger running-product + GCD arm to show the primitive-based sweep needs no bignum arithmetic at all.
problems.notes: 5 self-verified TheoryData cases (incl. [2,3,3]->0 from the problem's own illustrative text, and a 5-element case hand-checked via direct gcd factoring). Benchmark data drawn from a small shared-prime pool so no split is ever found early, forcing both arms through the full array (verified via a temporary smoke-check both arms agree at Length 200/2000, always -1).

problems.title: Check Knight Tour Configuration
problems.primitivesUsed: None - direct array indexing (order->cell inverse lookup + fixed knight-offset check). Same 'no repo Representation/Operations primitive is a genuine fit' precedent already established and documented by AvailableCapturesForRookTests/Benchmarks: Grid/GridChildren models only unordered single-step orthogonal adjacency for graph walks, not a knight's two-over-one-across offset set, so forcing this through Grid/** would be a non-fit, not a missing primitive.
problems.notes: 4 test cases, all independently verified (not from memory): trivial 1x1, an obviously-invalid row-major 3x3, and a genuine 5x5 open knight's tour generated and checked by a backtracking script (plus that same tour with two order values swapped to break it). Benchmark uses two verified real tours (5x5, 7x7, generated via Warnsdorff's heuristic and checked) so neither arm exits early - n itself is capped at <=7 by the problem's own constraint. Both arms cross-checked equal via a temporary smoke-check.

problems.title: The Number of Beautiful Subsets
problems.primitivesUsed: Algorithms.Backtracking.Backtrack.Search (same 'fold the legality rule into Candidates instead of generate-then-filter' shape as BeautifulArrangementTests/NumberOfValidMoveCombinationsOnChessboardTests) composed with DataStructures.HashMap<int,int> as a running value-frequency map, giving an O(1) two-lookup legality check per include decision.
problems.notes: 4 self-verified TheoryData cases by hand (incl. a duplicate-value case [1,1],k=1->3 to prove index-based, not value-based, subset counting - duplicates never conflict with each other since |x-x|=0<k). Benchmark's bitmask-generate-then-filter baseline and the pruned-Backtrack arm cross-checked equal via a temporary smoke-check at Length 12 and 16.

problems.title: Collect Coins in a Tree
problems.primitivesUsed: DataStructures.Queue.Queue<int> as the leaf-peeling BFS frontier over plain adjacency lists (RepoQueue-aliased to avoid the BCL Queue<T> name collision). Baseline arm rescans all nodes each round instead of using the queue.
problems.notes: Editorial reduction verified by hand against both official examples: fixed-point-trim leaves with coins==0, then peel two more unconditional leaf layers (radius-2 free-collection rule), answer = 2 * remaining edges. No new production primitive needed - TopologicalSort.TrySort doesn't fit (it's in-degree/DAG-oriented and runs to exhaustion; this needs undirected degree with a coin-gated first round and an early, non-exhaustive stop), so the peel is hand-written using the repo's own Queue<int>, matching the established MinimumHeightTreesTests.cs precedent for this exact shape.

problems.title: Minimum Reverse Operations
problems.primitivesUsed: Algorithms.Reducing.Reduce.Graph (BreadthFirstReduceOrder + DistanceMapReduceAlgebra) over a custom IGraphTopology/IChildren pair (ReversalTopology/ReversalChildren, in Fixtures/, mirroring Domain.Grids' GridNode/GridChildren on-demand-computed-adjacency pattern) plus DataStructures.Set<int> for banned positions.
problems.notes: Considered the classic DSU 'next available slot' trick (which this repo's DisjointSet primitive looks suited for) but rejected it: DisjointSet.Union is unconditionally union-by-rank, and that trick requires the caller to control which side survives as root (always the higher/still-available index) - rank can be bumped by unrelated prior merges, so a rank-based union silently breaks the required monotonic-successor invariant. Used Reduce.Graph with children computed directly from the reversal-window arithmetic instead (O(k) per node), verified exactly against all 3 official examples including the two banned-position edge cases.

problems.title: Minimum Number of Visited Cells in a Grid
problems.primitivesUsed: Algorithms.Reducing.Reduce.Graph (BreadthFirstReduceOrder + DistanceMapReduceAlgebra) over a custom IGraphTopology/IChildren pair (JumpGridTopology/JumpGridChildren, in Fixtures/) computing each cell's rightward/downward jump range on demand - the same 'geometry-computed representation' pattern Domain.Grids.GridChildren already established, just for a jump-range rule instead of 4-directional adjacency, so the existing production GridNode/GridChildren/GridTopology were left untouched rather than repurposed.
problems.notes: Verified against all 3 official examples, including the unreachable-target case (grid=[[2,1,0],[1,0,0]] -> -1), by hand-tracing reachability. Answer is distance+1 since LeetCode counts visited cells, not edges.

problems.title: Design Graph With Shortest Path Calculator
problems.primitivesUsed: Algorithms.ShortestPaths.ShortestPath.Dijkstra (Collections.Heap-backed frontier) + DataStructures.Graph.Contracts.Ordering.ListEdges<TNode,TEdgeData> + a local IEdgeTopology witness over a mutable per-node edge List<(int Weight, Node Target)> - same WeightedNode/ListEdges/IEdgeTopology composition NetworkDelayTimeTests (LC 743) already uses; AddEdge is a plain List.Add, ShortestPathBetween re-runs Dijkstra fresh from node1 each query since addEdge can mutate the graph between calls.
problems.notes: Test: two Facts, one walking AddEdge growing the graph and re-querying, one for the all-isolated-nodes case. Benchmark contrasts a naive O(V^2) array Dijkstra baseline vs. the repo's Heap-backed ShortestPath.Dijkstra across 200 random-source queries per graph size (50, 200 nodes) on the existing RandomWeightedGraphs/WeightedGraphNode/WeightedGraphTopology fixtures (shared with ShortestPathAlgorithmBenchmarks/CourseScheduleIVBenchmarks). Both projects build clean; xUnit tests pass (2/2); benchmark arms cross-verified equal via a standalone smoke harness (both report reached=10000 at n=50, 40000 at n=200). Query method deliberately named ShortestPathBetween (not literal shortestPath) to avoid shadowing the imported ShortestPath static class inside its own call site.

problems.title: Minimum Number of Operations to Make All Array Elements Equal to 1
problems.primitivesUsed: None from DataStructures/Algorithms - Bezout's identity reduces this to finding the shortest contiguous window whose own gcd is 1 (answer n-ones if a 1 is already present), the same 'nothing to compose over a running integer fold' shape this repo already establishes as done (not blocked) in CheckIfItIsAGoodArrayTests/FindGreatestCommonDivisorOfArrayTests/ReplaceNonCoprimeNumbersInArrayTests, which explicitly state 'no repo container or algorithm primitive applies here' and reuse the same private Euclidean Gcd one-liner inline. This problem drives that identical helper through an O(n^2) window scan instead of a single O(n) fold.
problems.notes: Test: 3 Facts (no-initial-one example verified by hand to answer 4, overall-gcd-not-1 returns -1, already-all-ones returns 0). Benchmark mirrors CheckIfItIsAGoodArrayBenchmarks'/FindGreatestCommonDivisorOfArrayBenchmarks' subtraction-vs-Euclidean Gcd contrast applied to the O(n^2) scan; values kept as multiples of 6 so no window ever reaches gcd 1, forcing both arms through the full scan. Both projects build clean; xUnit tests pass (3/3); benchmark arms cross-verified equal via smoke harness (both -1 at length 30 and 100, as designed).

problems.title: Maximum Number of Fish in a Grid
problems.primitivesUsed: Algorithms.Traversal.DepthFirst.DepthFirstSearch.Traverse over a bare (row,col) successor function - the same border-agnostic flood-fill primitive MaxAreaOfIslandTests/NumberOfIslandsTests already use for LC 695/200, here treating grid[r][c] > 0 as water and summing each visited cell's own fish count instead of using the traversal's List<TNode>.Count as an island's area.
problems.notes: Test: classic hand-verified example (max component sum 7) plus all-land edge case. Benchmark mirrors MaxAreaOfIslandBenchmarks' shape (hand-specialized recursive flood fill vs. DepthFirstSearch.Traverse) summing fish per component instead of counting cells, across two grid sides (30, 120). Both projects build clean; xUnit tests pass (2/2); benchmark arms cross-verified equal via smoke harness. Had to explicitly name the DFS start tuple (Row: r, Col: c) - an unnamed (r, c) literal makes C# infer element names r/c onto the traversal's result type, breaking .Row/.Col access downstream.

problems.title: Make Array Empty
problems.primitivesUsed: DSAExperimentation.DataStructures.FenwickTree.FenwickTree<int,SumOperation<int>> (Binary Indexed Tree): the circular remove-or-move-to-back simulation is reframed as processing original indices in ascending value order and, for each one, counting still-present slots between the previous removal and this one (wrapping around) via the Fenwick tree's point Add + range Query - O(log n) per step instead of an O(n) linear scan.
problems.notes: 3 LeetCode examples ([3,4,-1]->5, [1,2,4,3]->5, [1,2,3]->3, hand-verified by tracing the algorithm) plus a single-element edge case. Test file runs both a plain O(n)-per-step linear-scan version and the Fenwick version as a correctness cross-check, mirroring CountGoodTripletsInAnArrayTests' shape. Benchmark pairs LinearScan (baseline) vs FenwickTreeSweep at Length=200/5000 on a shuffled-distinct-values input; dry-run smoke test showed 29.3ms -> 4.7ms at Length=5000, confirming the expected O(n^2)-total vs O(n log n)-total split. Full build (dotnet build, both Debug and Release) and `dotnet test` (13/13 passing incl. this cluster) verified; benchmark verified with a BenchmarkDotNet --job Dry smoke run (no exceptions, correct answers, sane ratios).

problems.title: Minimum Cost of a Path With Special Roads
problems.primitivesUsed: DSAExperimentation.Algorithms.ShortestPaths.ShortestPath.Dijkstra over the graph contracts IEdgeTopology/ListEdges<TNode,int> (DataStructures/Graph/Contracts/Ordering). Tests side reuses the existing WeightedNode/WeightedTopology fixtures (DSAExperimentation.Tests.Algorithms.ShortestPaths.Fixtures) that NetworkDelayTimeTests already uses for LC 743; Benchmarks side reuses the existing WeightedGraphNode/WeightedGraphTopology fixtures (DSAExperimentation.Benchmarks.Fixtures) used by the Dijkstra/BellmanFord/FloydWarshall benchmarks. start/target/each special road's two endpoints become graph nodes, wired with a direct Manhattan-distance edge between every pair (you can always walk directly for that cost) plus each special road's own one-way discounted edge; Dijkstra's settled distance to the target node is the answer.
problems.notes: 1 official LeetCode example (start=[1,1], target=[4,5], 2 chained special roads -> 5, hand-traced through the graph) plus 2 custom hand-verified scenarios (an overpriced special road correctly ignored in favor of direct Manhattan distance; a single special road taken as a direct discounted shortcut). No new fixtures needed - both Tests' and Benchmarks' weighted-graph fixtures already existed. Benchmark compares a textbook O(V^2) array-scan Dijkstra (no priority queue, edges computed on the fly from the Manhattan formula) against ShortestPath.Dijkstra's heap-based version at SpecialRoadCount=20/100; on this dense near-complete graph the array-scan baseline legitimately wins (documented in the benchmark's own comment as the expected dense-graph trade-off) - the benchmark's purpose is proving Dijkstra's correctness/composability for this problem, not winning the race. Full build (Debug+Release) and `dotnet test` (13/13 passing incl. this cluster) verified; benchmark verified with a BenchmarkDotNet --job Dry smoke run (no exceptions, correct-looking answers).

problems.title: Frequency Tracker
problems.primitivesUsed: Two instances of DSAExperimentation.DataStructures.HashMap.HashMap<int,int> - the classic 'frequency of frequencies' technique, the same composition DesignHashMapTests already establishes for wrapping HashMap<TKey,TValue> as a LeetCode design problem. One map tracks each number's current count; the other tracks how many distinct numbers currently sit at each frequency. Add/DeleteOne move a number's count by one and mirror that move into the frequency map (decrement the old frequency bucket, increment the new one); HasFrequency is a single presence/count check on the second map.
problems.notes: 3 tests: LeetCode's own add/hasFrequency example sequence, a delete-of-a-number-never-added no-op (and confirms hasFrequency(0) stays false), and a delete-back-to-a-previous-frequency case verifying both frequency buckets update correctly. Follows MinStackTests/DesignHashMapTests' nested '<Name>Operations' class shape. Benchmark pairs SortedScanList (the 'no hashing at all' baseline - IndexOf-based delete plus a sort-and-run-length-scan HasFrequency, mirroring DesignHashMapBenchmarks' naive-baseline philosophy for LC 706) vs RepoHashMap at Length=200/5000; dry-run smoke test showed 56.9ms -> 3.6ms at Length=5000. Full build (Debug+Release) and `dotnet test` (13/13 passing incl. this cluster) verified; benchmark verified with a BenchmarkDotNet --job Dry smoke run (no exceptions, correct answers, sane ratios).

problems.title: Count the Number of Complete Components
problems.primitivesUsed: DataStructures.DisjointSet.DisjointSet (Union/Find) to group nodes into components, then a per-root node-count/edge-count tally checked against n*(n-1)/2 to test completeness.
problems.notes: Benchmark compares a BFS-collected-component + O(k^2) pairwise adjacency-set scan (naive) against the DisjointSet tally (primitive) over disjoint 25-node cliques; at NodeCount=2500 the DisjointSet arm is faster (3.6ms vs 5.4ms) and allocates ~1% as much. Both projects build clean and all 8 new xUnit facts pass.

problems.title: Modify Graph Edge Weights
problems.primitivesUsed: Algorithms.ShortestPaths.ShortestPath.Dijkstra called repeatedly over a mutable WeightedNode graph (the same fixture NetworkDelayTimeTests uses) - each -1 edge's ListEdges-backed entry is mutated in place between Dijkstra passes to grow its weight toward target.
problems.notes: Test reuses DSAExperimentation.Tests' internal WeightedNode/WeightedTopology fixtures (ListEdges wraps the node's own List<> by reference, so editing Edges[i] in place and re-running Dijkstra is sufficient - no mutable-edge-weight primitive needed). Hand-derived examples (floor-below-target stretch, floor-already-exact, floor-above-target impossible, multi -1-edge) all verified by manual Dijkstra trace before writing, and all pass. Benchmark contrasts an O(target) linear weight-search baseline against the O(1)-Dijkstra-pass formula approach on a chain graph; smoke-verified via a BenchmarkDotNet Dry run (allocation scales with StretchAmount for the naive arm, near-zero for the formula arm).

problems.title: Extra Characters in a String
problems.primitivesUsed: DataStructures.Trie.Trie<bool> for prefix-pruned dictionary lookup + Algorithms.DynamicProgramming.Memoizer for the top-down memoized recurrence - the exact same primitive pair DSAExperimentation.Tests/LeetCodeCoverage/WordBreak already proves out, here minimizing a leftover-character count instead of returning reachability.
problems.notes: Benchmark contrasts a HashSet<string> full O(n^2) substring scan (naive) against the Trie-pruned scan (primitive); Dry-run smoke test at Length=1500 showed 144ms/1.1MB (naive) vs 3.15ms/204KB (Trie), a clear, correctly-signed gap.

problems.title: Greatest Common Divisor Traversal
problems.primitivesUsed: DataStructures.DisjointSet.DisjointSet + DataStructures.HashMap.HashMap<int,int> - same prime-factor-union composition as LargestComponentSizeByCommonFactorTests/GCDSortOfAnArrayTests: union index i with the first-seen index sharing any of nums[i]'s prime factors (trial-division factorization), then check every index lands in one component (gcd(a,b)>1 iff a,b share a prime factor).
problems.notes: Build succeeded (0 warnings/errors), dotnet test green (5/5 new facts/theories: 3 real LeetCode examples + 2 edge cases). Benchmark's PairwiseGcdScan baseline and DisjointSetByPrimeFactor arm cross-checked to return identical answers at Length=50/400 via a throwaway console harness.

problems.title: Maximum Strictly Increasing Cells in a Matrix
problems.primitivesUsed: Algorithms.Sorting.MergeSort + DataStructures.Sequence.ArrayIndexedSequence - same sort-then-batch convention as RankTransformOfAMatrixTests: sort every cell by value once, process each equal-value batch together (dp = 1 + max(rowBest[row], colBest[col]) computed from pre-batch state, folded back in after), answer = max over the final rowBest/colBest arrays. No DisjointSet needed here since there's no tie-rank chaining to resolve, just row/column running maxima.
problems.notes: Build succeeded, dotnet test green (4/4 new facts, including 2 that reproduce LeetCode's own published examples, hand-simulated to confirm correctness). Benchmark's MemoizedRowColumnScan (O(rows*cols*(rows+cols)) DAG-DP baseline) and SortedBatchDp arm cross-checked equal at Size=8/20.

problems.title: Maximum Sum Queries
problems.primitivesUsed: DataStructures.SegmentTree.SegmentTree<long,MaxOperation<long>> + Algorithms.Searching.BinarySearch.LowerBound + Algorithms.Sorting.MergeSort - same SegmentTree+BinarySearch coordinate-compression composition BookingConcertTicketsInGroupsTests already proves out: coordinate-compress nums2's distinct values, sweep indices and queries together sorted descending by nums1/x, admit indices into the segment tree keyed by nums2's compressed rank as their nums1 threshold is met, answer each query with one range-max query over [LowerBound(y), lastRank]; MaxOperation's own Identity (long.MinValue) sentinel makes -1 fall out with no extra bookkeeping.
problems.notes: Build succeeded, dotnet test green (3/3 new facts, including LeetCode's own published Example 1, hand-simulated step by step to confirm correctness plus 2 self-constructed boundary edge cases). Benchmark's O(n*q) BruteForceScan baseline and SweepWithSegmentTree arm cross-checked to return identical answer arrays across Length x QueryCount in {200,2000}^2 via a throwaway console harness.

problems.title: Special Permutations
problems.primitivesUsed: Algorithms.Backtracking.Backtrack.Search (brute-force full-permutation enumeration, PermutationsTests precedent) + Algorithms.DynamicProgramming.Memoizer (single-call bitmask DP over (Remaining, Last) state, Last=-1 seeding the empty-prefix start so one Memoize call sums every valid completion of every valid first choice - the same (Mask,Last) TSP-style state FindTheShortestSuperstringTests already establishes).
problems.notes: Build succeeded (Tests + Benchmarks projects, 0 warnings/errors). dotnet test green: 8/8 new facts (4 shared examples x 2 strategies via TheoryData, brute force and bitmask memo cross-verified against each other), including LeetCode's own two published examples plus a 2-element boundary case and a no-special-permutation-exists case, hand-derived and hand-simulated.

problems.title: Robot Collisions
problems.primitivesUsed: Algorithms.Sorting.MergeSort over DataStructures.Sequence.ArrayIndexedSequence with a custom (Position,Index) comparer (QueueReconstructionByHeightTests precedent) to establish position order, then DataStructures.Stack.Stack<int> for a single left-to-right sweep - AsteroidCollisionTests' stack-based collision simulation generalized from pure destroy/survive to health-bearing collisions (loser zeroed, survivor loses 1 health, ties destroy both).
problems.notes: Build succeeded. dotnet test green: 3/3 new facts - LeetCode's own 'no collisions, same direction' example, LeetCode's own 'RLRL' example (hand-simulated step by step: idx1/idx0 mutually destroy idx... resolves to [14]), and a custom cascading case where one high-health left-mover destroys three right-movers in sequence, losing 1 health per kill, hand-verified to [7].

problems.title: Continuous Subarrays
problems.primitivesUsed: Two DataStructures.Deque.Deque<int> instances as monotonic index windows (one decreasing-value for running max, one increasing-value for running min) - the exact LongestContinuousSubarrayWithAbsoluteDiffLessThanOrEqualToLimitTests mechanism with Limit fixed at 2, summing (right-left+1) at every right instead of tracking the single longest window.
problems.notes: Build succeeded. dotnet test green: 4/4 new facts - both LeetCode published examples (hand-simulated the first, [5,4,2,4] -> 8, step by step through window shrink/grow), an all-equal-values case (n*(n+1)/2 sanity check), and a single-element case.

problems.title: Maximum Number of Groups With Increasing Length
problems.primitivesUsed: MergeSort.Sort over ArrayIndexedSequence<int> (Algorithms/Sorting, DataStructures/Sequence) to sort usageLimits ascending, then a plain O(n) greedy accumulation sweep (exchange-argument proof: process smallest limits first). Benchmark contrasts a textbook O(n^2) insertion sort with the repo's O(n log n) MergeSort, both followed by the identical greedy sweep.

problems.title: Insert Greatest Common Divisors in Linked List
problems.primitivesUsed: SinglyLinkedListNode<T> (DataStructures/SinglyLinkedList) rewired in place to splice a new gcd node between each adjacent pair, plus an inlined Euclidean-algorithm private helper (same no-repo-primitive-applies precedent FindGreatestCommonDivisorOfArrayTests already established for two-integer GCD). Benchmark contrasts rebuilding via an intermediate List<int> vs. in-place node splicing.

problems.title: Minimum Time to Make Array Sum At Most x
problems.primitivesUsed: MergeSort.Sort over ArrayIndexedSequence<(int,int)> (Algorithms/Sorting, DataStructures/Sequence) to sort (nums1,nums2) pairs ascending by nums2, then a plain 0/1-knapsack-shaped DP loop (same 'write the DP directly, no dedicated repo primitive needed' precedent as JumpGameVI/LongestIncreasingSubsequenceII/ConstrainedSubsequenceSum) to compute max reduction per operation count. Benchmark contrasts a dense O(n^2)-space 2D DP table (with BCL Array.Sort) against the repo-MergeSort-backed O(n)-space rolling-array DP - both O(n^2) time, the primitive approach O(n) space.

problems.title: Faulty Keyboard
problems.primitivesUsed: DataStructures.Deque.Deque<char> (DSAExperimentation/LeetCode/FaultyKeyboard/FaultyKeyboardSolution.cs, method FinalStringByDeque): 'i' just flips which end subsequent characters are pushed to (PushFront/PushBack), so the reversal never actually happens; the buffer is read back out with TryPopFront or TryPopBack depending on final orientation. Baseline (FinalStringByReversal) does the literal List<char>.Reverse() on every 'i'. Verified against both official LeetCode examples (both strategies match); benchmark smoke-tested with a BenchmarkDotNet Dry job at Length=200/5000 (no exceptions).

problems.title: Find the Safest Path in a Grid
problems.primitivesUsed: DSAExperimentation/LeetCode/FindTheSafestPathInAGrid/FindTheSafestPathInAGridSolution.cs, method MaximumSafenessFactorByHeap composes: DataStructures.Queue.Queue<T> for the multi-source BFS that computes each cell's safeness (Manhattan distance to nearest thief) - same technique as the existing ZeroOneMatrix coverage; DataStructures.Heap.Heap<T,TOrder> + Graph.ShortestPaths.ByPriorityOrder<TNode,TWeight> (negating the priority turns the fixed min-heap comparison into a max-heap, avoiding any new IHeapOrder witness) driving a modified-Dijkstra 'maximum bottleneck path' walk over Graph.Grids' GridNode/GridTopology/GridChildren/Grid (all-passable, same move MaximumNumberOfPointsFromGridQueries's coverage test uses) for 4-directional neighbor iteration. Baseline (MaximumSafenessFactorByBclBfs) is a hand-rolled BCL Queue-based multi-source BFS plus binary search over the safeness threshold with a hand-rolled BCL Queue-based reachability BFS per step - a genuinely different algorithm, not just a primitive swap. Verified by hand-tracing the heap walk against all 3 official LeetCode examples (including the diagonal-thieves case where the naive upper bound of 3 is unreachable and the true answer is 2) and confirmed by the passing test suite; benchmark smoke-tested with a Dry job at Size=20/80 (no exceptions, sensible timings).

problems.title: Maximum Elegance of a K-Length Subsequence
problems.primitivesUsed: DSAExperimentation/LeetCode/MaximumEleganceOfAKLengthSubsequence/MaximumEleganceOfAKLengthSubsequenceSolution.cs, method MaximumEleganceByRepoPrimitives composes: Algorithms.Sorting.MergeSort.Sort over DataStructures.Sequence.ArrayIndexedSequence<T> to sort items by profit descending (same composition as the existing TheNumberOfWeakCharactersInTheGame coverage test), DataStructures.Set.Set<int> to track seen categories, and DataStructures.Stack.Stack<int> (aliased via 'using RepoProfitStack = ...' to dodge the known CS0104 collision with System.Collections.Generic.Stack<T> from this project's global usings) as the LIFO stack of replaceable duplicate-category profits for the standard greedy-swap algorithm. Baseline (MaximumEleganceByBcl) is the same algorithm over OrderByDescending/HashSet<int>/BCL Stack<int>. Verified by hand-computing the greedy-swap trace against all 3 official LeetCode examples (17, 19, 7) matching exactly, confirmed by the passing test suite; benchmark smoke-tested with a Dry job at ItemCount=500/5000 (no exceptions).

problems.title: Double a Number Represented as a Linked List
problems.primitivesUsed: DSAExperimentation.DataStructures.SinglyLinkedList.SinglyLinkedListNode<TValue> + DSAExperimentation.DataStructures.Stack.Stack<int>. Same digit-reversal-via-stack composition AddTwoNumbersIITests already uses (digits stored most-significant-first), applied to a single operand doubled against itself instead of two operands summed: push every digit walking .Next once, then pop least-significant-first with a running carry, prepending each doubled digit.
problems.notes: 3/3 new xUnit tests pass (LeetCode's 189->378, 999->1998, and a single-zero edge case). problems.title: String Transformation

ZFunction.FindAll (a cross-referential Z-search, no concatenation/sentinel needed) computes that count in O(n) over `s + s[0..n-1]` (every length-n window is one left-rotation of s); benchmark/test both compare it against an O(n^2) direct window-compare brute force.

problems.title: Maximum Strong Pair XOR I
problems.primitivesUsed: DataStructures/Graph/Engines/Dags/Trees/BitTrie.cs (insert + greedy max-XOR walk); Algorithms/Sorting/MergeSort.cs + DataStructures/Sequence/ArrayIndexedSequence.cs (hoisted pre-sorted overload, mirrors the LC 1707 offline-sweep composition already in the repo). Two strategies: MaximumStrongPairXorByBruteForce (O(n^2) textbook) and MaximumStrongPairXorByBitTrieBuckets (sort + bucket-by-highest-set-bit + insert-only BitTrie sweep across same/adjacent buckets - no trie removal needed, proven correct against LeetCode examples plus a 2000-trial randomized stress test against brute force).
problems.notes: Same underlying function as LC 2935 at a smaller bound; both strategies proven here too, matching the DistributeCandiesAmongChildrenI/II precedent of duplicating both strategies across the I/II split rather than gating the smart one to only the harder problem.

problems.title: Maximum Strong Pair XOR II
problems.primitivesUsed: Same as 2932: DataStructures/Graph/Engines/Dags/Trees/BitTrie.cs, Algorithms/Sorting/MergeSort.cs, DataStructures/Sequence/ArrayIndexedSequence.cs. No new Domain/ or LeetCode-local witness type needed - ArrayIndexedSequence<int> (not IEnumerable<int>) already serves as the disambiguated 'pre-sorted' hoisted-overload parameter per ARCHITECTURE.md 17.4.
problems.notes: The obvious editorial approach (sort + two-pointer window that shrinks on the left, removing stale elements from a shared trie) is NOT what's implemented, because BitTrie is insert-only with no delete - that would have been a genuine primitive gap. Instead this composes a provably equivalent insert-only algorithm: group sorted nums into buckets by highest set bit (2^k <= v < 2^(k+1)); within a bucket every pair is automatically a strong pair (reduces to LC 421's Maximum XOR of Two Numbers, same BitTrie composition MaximumXOROfTwoNumbersInAnArrayTests already uses); across adjacent buckets only, walk the lower bucket ascending and insert upper-bucket elements into a second BitTrie via a monotonically GROWING two-pointer (never shrinks, since the eligibility threshold 2x only grows as x grows) - the same offline-sweep shape MaximumXORWithAnElementFromArrayTests (LC 1707) already uses in this repo, just keyed by 2x instead of a query limit. Pairs more than one bucket apart are proven impossible (2x < 2^m <= y). Verified against LeetCode's published examples plus a 2000-trial randomized stress test comparing against the brute-force baseline - no disagreements.

problems.title: Find Building Where Alice and Bob Can Meet
problems.primitivesUsed: DataStructures/Heap/Heap.cs with MinHeapOrder<(int,int)> as the offline sweep's priority queue (keyed by (threshold height, query index), using ValueTuple's built-in IComparable); LeetCode/LeetCodeAnswer.None for the 'no valid meeting building' sentinel. No new Domain/ types needed.
problems.notes: Classic offline min-heap sweep: each query normalizes to lo=min(a,b), hi=max(a,b); lo==hi and heights[lo]<heights[hi] resolve immediately, everything else is bucketed by its hi index with threshold=heights[lo]. A single left-to-right sweep over the buildings pops every heap entry whose threshold the current index clears (answering it there) before pushing that index's own newly-bucketed queries. Since LeetCode's own published example numbers couldn't be verified without network access, the test's TheoryData uses two hand-derived-and-hand-verified scenarios (covering the trivial/direct-jump/near-fallback/far-fallback/unreachable/index-order-invariance branches) rather than risk misquoting the source examples from memory; a 2000-trial randomized stress test against the brute-force baseline found zero disagreements, corroborating both the hand-worked examples and the algorithm.

New problem-scoped TimedAdjacency.cs witness (adjacency-list construction) added to the LeetCode/ folder; DSAExperimentation.Benchmarks/Fixtures/DisappearingNodesWorkloads.cs for workload sizing. problems.primitivesUsed: DataStructures.HashMap.HashMap<int,int> - two instances tallying ones per row and per column, the same row/column-tally shape an existing (unmigrated) CountServersThatCommunicate test uses for LC 1267, here with this repo's own HashMap instead of a BCL Dictionary. Every 1-cell is a potential right-angle corner contributing (row tally - 1) * (column tally - 1) triangles; summing that over all 1-cells (verified by hand against all three published examples: 2, 0, 2) is the composed CountByTalliedRowsAndColumns strategy. Baseline CountByBruteForceRowColumnScan rescans each corner's whole row/column from scratch every time (no tallying), deliberately with no repo primitive, per Section 17.5. New Benchmarks/Fixtures/RightTriangleWorkloads.cs builds a random square 0/1 grid (workload sizing only, mirrors DigitGridWorkloads' existing shape for LC 3044). Return type is long to match LeetCode's own metaData (grid up to 1000x1000, so the corner-product sum can exceed int range). All three projects build clean; 6 Theory cases pass; a Dry-job benchmark run executes both arms without error.

problems.title: Find the Minimum Cost Array Permutation
problems.primitivesUsed: Algorithms.DynamicProgramming.Memoizer, composed over bitmask-TSP state (Mask, Last) - the same (Mask, Last)-over-Memoizer shape an existing (unmigrated) FindTheShortestSuperstring test uses for its own Hamiltonian-path DP (LC 943), here minimizing |perm[i]-nums[perm[i+1]]| instead of maximizing string overlap. Since the score is a rotation-invariant sum around a cycle, the lexicographically smallest optimum always starts at label 0 (proved in the solution's doc comment), so the DP fixes perm[0]=0 and computes g(mask,last) = minimum cost to complete the tour; reconstruction greedily picks, at each step, the smallest unvisited candidate whose edge cost plus completion cost matches the state's optimum, which yields the lexicographically smallest minimum-cost permutation. Verified by hand against both published examples (nums=[1,0,2]->[0,1,2], nums=[0,2,1]->[0,2,1]). Baseline FindPermutationByBruteForceSearch is plain BCL swap-based backtracking over all n! permutations scored directly against the problem's own cyclic formula, deliberately with no repo primitive and without the 'start at 0' shortcut, per Section 17.5. Benchmark workload (a random permutation) is built inline in [GlobalSetup] rather than in Fixtures/, matching the existing AddTwoNumbersBenchmarks precedent for workload sizing that fixes no domain content. All three projects build clean; 4 Theory cases pass; a Dry-job benchmark run executes both arms without error (and visibly shows the O(n!) baseline overtaking the bitmask strategy between n=6 and n=8).
