No Domain type needed; the k+1<stair prune (verified by hand against both LC examples) bounds recursion depth to O(log k) regardless of k.

problems.title: Block Placement Queries
problems.primitivesUsed: DataStructures.SegmentTree.SegmentTree<long,MaxOperation<long>> for the prefix-max-gap query, plus DataStructures.DisjointSet.DisjointSetForest (the raw parent-array representation) driven by this problem's own NearestActiveObstacle.cs, a directional path-compressed Find written against the forest directly because DisjointSet's own Union is rank-based/undirected and cannot express the fixed-direction 'deactivate toward this neighbor' merge the reverse-time offline technique needs. Algorithm (queries processed in reverse, each type-1 becomes a deactivation/merge) was hand-verified against both LC examples then cross-checked with a 300-trial randomized stress test against a brute-force oracle before porting to C#.

problems.title: Maximum Sum of Subsequence With Non-adjacent Elements
problems.primitivesUsed: DataStructures.SegmentTree.SegmentTree<Element,TOperation> generically reused with a new problem-local ICombineOperation witness (NonAdjacentMergeOperation.cs / NonAdjacentSumNode.cs, the classic 4-value boundary-constrained DP merge for point-updatable House Robber), plus Domain.Modular.ModularArithmetic.Modulo for the 1e9+7 reduction. Merge algebra hand-derived and simulated in Python against both LC examples before porting to C#.

problems.title: Find Subarray With Bitwise OR Closest to K
problems.primitivesUsed: No named DataStructures/Algorithms types needed - MinimumDifferenceByBruteForce is a plain O(n^2) BCL scan; MinimumDifferenceByOrCompression composes only BCL List<int>, implementing the standard 'distinct-OR-suffixes' technique (each right endpoint keeps a strictly-increasing, O(log(max value))-sized list of OR values for subarrays ending there, since submask <= superset bounds the chain length by bit count). No Domain/ reuse.

problems.title: Find the N-th Value After K Seconds
problems.primitivesUsed: Domain.Modular.ModularArithmetic (Modulo constant + Inverse/Power) reused for the closed-form strategy: a[n-1] after k seconds is C(n-1+k, k), computed as a factorial ratio via ModularArithmetic.Inverse for the modular denominator. Brute-force arm is a plain O(n*k) BCL simulation using the same Modulo constant.

problems.title: Peaks in Array
problems.primitivesUsed: DataStructures/FenwickTree/FenwickTree<int, SumOperation<int>> (point-update/range-query Fenwick tree, the same composition DistributeElementsIntoTwoArraysIISolution already uses) stores a 0/1 peak indicator per index; a type-1 query is Query(l+1, r-1) and a type-2 update removes/re-adds indicators only at index-1, index, index+1 (the only positions an update can affect). Brute-force arm rescans the range directly with a plain BCL int[].

problems.title: Minimum Operations to Make Binary Array Elements Equal to One I
problems.primitivesUsed: DataStructures/Queue/Queue<int> (aliased FlipStartQueue) tracks the >=2 still-active flip starts for the O(1)-extra-space strategy; baseline arm is plain BCL array mutation. No new production types.

problems.title: Number of Subarrays With AND Value of K
problems.primitivesUsed: DataStructures/HashMap/HashMap<int,long> merges the <=30 distinct AND-values ending at each index (AND-value-compression strategy); baseline is a plain O(n^2) BCL scan. No new production types.

problems.title: Construct String with Minimum Cost
problems.primitivesUsed: DataStructures/AhoCorasick/AhoCorasick + AhoCorasickMatch drive the suffix-DP directly (every (position,matching word) pair the DP needs is exactly what FindAll reports, already sorted by Start); DataStructures/HashMap/HashMap<string,int> dedupes words to their min cost before building the automaton. Hoisted overload (string,AhoCorasick,IReadOnlyList<string>,int[]) per ARCHITECTURE.md 17.4 so benchmark GlobalSetup charges automaton construction. Baseline is a plain O(n*words*len) substring-check DP. No new production types.

problems.title: Delete Nodes From Linked List Present in Array
problems.primitivesUsed: DataStructures.SinglyLinkedList.SinglyLinkedListNode<int> (same node type AddTwoNumbers uses) for the list; DataStructures.Set<int> for the composed strategy's O(1) nums membership check (hoisted overload per ARCHITECTURE.md 17.4), mirroring TwoSum's baseline-nested-scan (Array.IndexOf) vs. repo-container (Set.Has) shape. Both strategies are one dummy-head splice pass. No new primitive.
problems.notes: Benchmark rebuilds the list inside each [Benchmark] call from GlobalSetup-built value arrays (both strategies mutate .Next in place, so reusing one prebuilt list across iterations would corrupt later measurements); only the nums Set is hoisted to GlobalSetup. 6 tests pass; benchmark dry-run executes cleanly.

problems.title: Find the Winning Player in Coin Game
problems.primitivesUsed: None. 75 + 4*10 = 115 is the only coin combination reaching a turn's required value, so the whole problem reduces to min(x, y/4) turns and a parity check - no DSA primitive applies. Strategies: direct turn-by-turn simulation (baseline) vs. the derived O(1) formula (composed).
problems.notes: 4 tests pass; benchmark dry-run executes cleanly across (x,y) in {1,100}x{4,100}.

problems.title: Vowels Game in a String
problems.primitivesUsed: DataStructures.Set<char> holds the vowel set for the composed strategy's O(n) scan. Baseline is a from-scratch memoized recursive game-tree search (two mutually recursive per-role functions, since Alice's odd-vowel-substring moves and Bob's even-vowel-substring moves are not interchangeable) using a plain Dictionary<string,bool> memo - no repo primitive fits this bespoke asymmetric two-role game, so it stays BCL like other baselines (e.g. AddTwoNumbers's BigInteger arm). Before committing to the closed form, verified it against a from-scratch brute-force game solver over 3000 random small strings plus both official LeetCode examples - 0 mismatches - confirming the game always reduces to 'Alice wins iff s contains at least one vowel'.
problems.notes: 4 tests pass; benchmark dry-run executes cleanly at lengths 8 and 20 (kept intentionally small - the recursive game search's cost does not grow smoothly with n and can reach many thousands of states by length ~30-40 on adversarial mixed inputs, confirmed empirically before sizing the benchmark).

problems.title: Minimum Operations to Make Array Equal to Target
problems.primitivesUsed: No composed data structure - verified this is genuinely primitive-free: the optimal answer is the sum of positive steps of target[i]-nums[i] (with 0 sentinels), a single O(n) scan over plain arrays (MinOperationsByDifferenceScan). Tried fitting this repo's Stack<T> as a 'monotonic stack' alternate strategy and RangeFenwickTree as a difference-array structure first; both were rejected - the stack framing actually computes a WRONG answer on non-monotone diff sequences (verified by hand: H=[1,3,2,3] gives 5 via a naive open-layer stack vs the correct 4), and RangeFenwickTree is range-update/point-query, not operation-count minimization, so neither is a genuine fit. Baseline (MinOperationsByBruteForceSimulation) is a literal O(operations*n) simulation of the problem's own described operation, added as DSAExperimentation.Benchmarks/Fixtures/ArrayEqualToTargetWorkloads.cs for benchmark sizing. Both strategies verified against LeetCode's own two published examples (outputs 2 and 5, confirmed via WebSearch/WebFetch against github.com/doocs/leetcode) plus independent hand-traced cases.

problems.title: Check if the Rectangle Corner Is Reachable
problems.primitivesUsed: DataStructures.DisjointSet.DisjointSet (existing primitive, same composition pattern already used by DSAExperimentation.LeetCode/FindTheStringWithLCP/FindTheStringWithLCPSolution.cs) - circles union together on pairwise overlap plus two virtual boundary-group ids (LeftOrTop, BottomOrRight); the rectangle corner is unreachable iff those two ids end up connected. Baseline strategy (IsReachableByBoundaryFloodFill) reimplements the same grouping with a plain BCL Queue flood fill instead, so the two arms differ only in which repo/BCL structure decides connectivity - the same shape OpenTheLock's own two strategies already establish as precedented. Geometry helpers (circle-covers-corner, circle-touches-axis-aligned-edge, circle-overlaps-circle) are plain long-arithmetic squared-distance checks scoped to this problem's own LeetCode folder (no Domain/ type fits a bare circle-vs-rectangle-edge check; Domain/Grids is discrete-grid pathfinding, not this). Added DSAExperimentation.Benchmarks/Fixtures/RectangleCornerWorkloads.cs for benchmark sizing. Verified against 4 LeetCode-published examples fetched from github.com/doocs/leetcode, each independently hand-traced through the algorithm to confirm correctness.

problems.title: Shortest Distance After Road Addition Queries II
problems.primitivesUsed: DataStructures.IntervalSet.IntervalSet<int> (existing primitive) - each query [u,v] bypasses the closed range of interior cities [u+1,v-1]; IntervalSet's existing overlap-merge logic tracks the union of all bypassed ranges for free, and the answer after each query is (n-1) minus the total bypassed-city count, valid specifically because LC3244-II guarantees queries never partially overlap (only nest or stay disjoint) - the same guarantee IntervalSet's own merge semantics rely on being cheap. Baseline strategy (ShortestDistancesByAdjacencyBfs) is a plain BCL Queue-based fresh BFS per query, mirroring LC3243's small-n approach, added as the arm the IntervalSet strategy must justify itself against. Added DSAExperimentation.Benchmarks/Fixtures/RoadAdditionQueryWorkloads.cs, which recursively carves random queries that satisfy the non-crossing (nested-or-disjoint) constraint by construction. Verified against both LeetCode-published examples fetched from github.com/doocs/leetcode (outputs [3,2,1] and [1,1]).

problems.title: Alternating Groups III
problems.primitivesUsed: New problem-local helper AlternatingGroupsIII/AlternatingRunLedger.cs (not a new production primitive - a §17.3 problem-only witness) composes: DataStructures.DynamicArray<int> keeping bad (same-color-neighbor) edge positions sorted, with Algorithms.Searching.BinarySearch.LowerBound over a private IRandomAccessSequence<int> view for O(log n) predecessor/successor lookup - the identical 'sorted DynamicArray + BinarySearch.LowerBound, no second bisection loop' composition DataStructures.IntervalSet already uses; and two DataStructures.FenwickTree<Element, DataStructures.FenwickTree.SumOperation<Element>> instances (count-of-runs-by-length, sum-of-lengths-by-length) so a size query is two O(log n) PrefixQuery calls instead of a full-circle scan. Brute-force baseline arm uses only the BCL array LeetCode's own input already is. Verified against both LeetCode examples plus 40 randomized trials cross-checking both strategies agree, and a BenchmarkDotNet dry-run (Length=1000/5000) confirms the composed strategy scales far better (120ms->11ms vs baseline's near-linear growth) with no runtime exceptions.

problems.title: Find the Count of Monotonic Pairs I
problems.primitivesUsed: Domain.Modular.ModularArithmetic.Modulo (LeetCode's own 1e9+7 reporting convention) used by both strategies' arithmetic, exactly as CountTheNumberOfGoodPartitionsSolution's baseline arm already does. The DP itself (row-by-row over 'arr1[i]==j', each row a prefix sum of the row before it shifted by delta=max(0,nums[i]-nums[i-1])) needed no other DataStructures/Algorithms primitive - it composes directly over plain arrays, with the two strategies being O(n*maxValue^2) brute force vs O(n*maxValue) running-prefix-sum. Verified against both LeetCode examples plus 40 randomized cross-checks between the two strategies (all agree).

problems.title: Find the Count of Monotonic Pairs II
problems.primitivesUsed: Same recurrence and same primitive (Domain.Modular.ModularArithmetic.Modulo) as #3250 - Part II is the identical statement with nums[i] allowed up to 1000 instead of 50, so it exists as its own independent solution class per the WordLadder/WordLadderII precedent (no cross-folder reuse), not sharing code with FindTheCountOfMonotonicPairsISolution. Benchmark pushes maxValue to the full 1000 ceiling to show the O(n*maxValue^2) baseline losing to the O(n*maxValue) prefix-sum arm. Verified against both LeetCode examples plus 20 randomized cross-checks between the two strategies (all agree).

problems.title: Find the Largest Palindrome Divisible by K
problems.primitivesUsed: Algorithms.DynamicProgramming.Memoizer<TState,TResult> over tuple state (Position, NeededResidue) for a digit-DP feasibility walk - the exact 'tuple state, Memoizer.Memoize' composition NumberOfBeautifulIntegersInTheRangeSolution.CountByDigitDpMemo already established. Each half-digit position contributes d*weight[i] to the full palindrome's residue mod k (weight[i] = (10^i + 10^(n-1-i)) % k, precomputed via a plain pow10-mod-k table), so the DP never materializes an n-digit string (n up to 1e5). A side Dictionary<(Position,Needed),int> records the largest feasible digit per visited state so the greedy digit-by-digit replay after Memoize returns is O(h) with no re-derivation. LargestPalindromeByBruteForce is the baseline: plain recursion trying half-digits 9->0 in descending order, leaf-checking divisibility via string digit-walk mod k - no repo primitive, BCL only. No Domain/ type was needed (k stays <=9, no 1e9+7 modulus involved, so Domain.Modular.ModularArithmetic does not apply here).

problems.title: Count Almost Equal Pairs II
problems.primitivesUsed: Algorithms.Backtracking.Backtrack.TrySearch (the 'find one and quit' bounded-reachability contract) composed with a new problem-local witness SwapBudgetState (DSAExperimentation.LeetCode/CountAlmostEqualPairsII/SwapBudgetState.cs - answers only this problem, so it lives beside the solution per ARCHITECTURE.md 17.3, not in Domain/), mirroring GenerateParenthesesSolution.Backtrack.Search composition. Two numbers are 'almost equal' iff one reaches the other within 2 digit swaps after zero-padding both to width 7 (nums[i] < 1e7); a swap on either number is equivalent to a swap on the other, so the two-number budget collapses to a single-string bounded-swap reachability check. CountByBoundedSwapBruteForce is the baseline: hand-rolled O(width^4) exhaustive one- and two-swap materialization/comparison over plain strings, no repo primitive. Both strategies take a second string[]-of-padded overload (Pad is internal, not private, specifically so the benchmark's [GlobalSetup] can call it directly) per the hoisted-overload rule - int[] and string[] can never be ambiguous at a call site.

problems.title: Find the Count of Good Integers
problems.primitivesUsed: Algorithms.Backtracking.Backtrack.Search (the enumerate-everything contract) composed with a new problem-local witness PalindromeHalfState (DSAExperimentation.LeetCode/FindTheCountOfGoodIntegers/PalindromeHalfState.cs - answers only this problem, so it lives beside the solution per ARCHITECTURE.md 17.3, not in Domain/), mirroring GenerateParenthesesSolution.GenerateByBacktracking's composition. n <= 10 here (unlike LC 3260's n up to 1e5), so every k-palindromic n-digit number is enumerated directly via its half (h = ceil(n/2), <= 90000 leaves); results are grouped by sorted-digit signature (a 'good' integer is really a distinct digit multiset) and each distinct signature contributes a multinomial-coefficient arrangement count minus leading-zero arrangements, computed with plain factorial arithmetic (no modulus needed - LC's own return type is a plain long, not mod 1e9+7, so Domain.Modular.ModularArithmetic does not apply). CountByPalindromeEnumeration is the baseline: hand-rolled recursive half-digit enumeration, no repo primitive.

problems.title: Select Cells in Grid With Maximum Score
problems.primitivesUsed: DSAExperimentation.Algorithms.DynamicProgramming.Memoizer only. The problem is maximum-weight bipartite matching between rows and distinct values; re-indexing the naive row-first recursion's state by DISTINCT VALUE instead of by row shrinks the memoizable half of the state from an unbounded used-value set down to a <=10-bit row bitmask, which Memoizer.Memoize<(int ValueIndex, int RowMask), int> caches directly. Baseline (MaxScoreByBruteForceRecursion) is a plain BCL HashSet<int> backtracking walk; composed (MaxScoreByBitmaskMemoization) has a hoisted overload taking the precomputed rows-by-value grouping.
problems.strategies: MaxScoreByBruteForceRecursion (textbook row-by-row backtracking over a BCL HashSet<int> of used values, not memoizable over this state shape), MaxScoreByBitmaskMemoization (Memoizer over (ValueIndex, RowMask), with a hoisted overload taking the precomputed rows-by-value grouping)
problems.notes: Verified against LeetCode's own fetched examples (fetched live via the repo's existing LeetCodeApiClient GraphQL pattern, not from memory). All 4 projects build clean (Release); 4 new Theory cases plus the full LeetCodeCoverage suite (3087 tests) and LayeringTests all pass.

problems.title: Maximum Number of Moves to Kill All Pawns
problems.primitivesUsed: Algorithms.Reducing.Reduce.Graph + BreadthFirstReduceOrder + DistanceMapReduceAlgebra (reused unmodified, same composition GridShortestPath/OpenTheLock use) over a new problem-local IGraphTopology witness pair (KnightTopology/KnightChildren, since GridChildren's 4-orthogonal offsets don't fit a knight); these live in the LeetCode/ problem folder per ARCHITECTURE.md 17.3's 'witness used by this problem alone' allowance, not in DataStructures/, and reuse DataStructures.Graph.Grids' existing GridNode/Grid rather than a new node type. Algorithms.DynamicProgramming.Memoizer for the (Mask, Last) alternating min/max bitmask-TSP recursion.
problems.strategies: MaxMovesByBruteForceMinimax (textbook BCL Queue-based BFS per point of interest for the distance matrix, hand-rolled Dictionary-memoized minimax recursion - no repo primitives), MaxMovesByReduceGraphMinimax (Reduce.Graph over the new KnightTopology witness for distances, Memoizer for the minimax, with a hoisted overload taking a precomputed KnightDistances record)
problems.notes: Verified against LeetCode's own fetched examples (3, live-fetched, not from memory); hand-traced example 3 against the (Mask,Last) recurrence before running anything to catch a design error early. All 4 projects build clean (Release); 6 new Theory cases plus the full LeetCodeCoverage suite (3087 tests) and LayeringTests all pass.

problems.title: Find a Safe Walk Through a Grid
problems.primitivesUsed: Algorithms.ShortestPaths.ShortestPath.Dijkstra + DataStructures.Graph.Grids.WeightedGridNode/WeightedGridTopology (reused unmodified). WeightedGrid.Build's fixed unit-weight edges don't fit (edge weight here must be the destination cell's own 0/1 value), so the solution wires its own WeightedGridNode graph with that edge rule rather than reusing WeightedGrid.Build itself - same node/topology types, different edge weights.
problems.strategies: IsSafeByBruteForceArrayDijkstra (textbook O((mn)^2) Dijkstra: linear scan for the next unsettled minimum over a flat int[] distance array, no heap, no repo primitives), IsSafeByWeightedGridDijkstra (ShortestPath.Dijkstra over a cell-cost-weighted WeightedGridNode graph, with a hoisted overload taking the precomputed graph)
problems.notes: Verified against LeetCode's own fetched examples (3, live-fetched, not from memory), including the case where grid[0][0]=1 so the start cell's own cost has to be added back onto Dijkstra's distance (which only ever charges weight to entering a destination, never the source). All 4 projects build clean (Release); 6 new Theory cases plus the full LeetCodeCoverage suite (3087 tests) and LayeringTests all pass.

problems.title: Length of the Longest Increasing Path
problems.primitivesUsed: DSAExperimentation.DataStructures.SegmentTree.SegmentTree<int, MaxOperation<int>> (point-update/range-max query) composed with Algorithms.Searching.BinarySearch.LowerBound over an ArraySequence<long> for y coordinate-compression - the exact 'compress + segment-tree sweep' idiom MaximumBalancedSubsequenceSumSolution already established. The answer is (longest chain ending at k) + (longest chain starting at k) - 1; both halves are computed by one shared private ChainLengths(points) helper, called once on the coordinates as given and once on their negation (reversing a chain preserves its length, so 'starts at i extending toward larger x,y' becomes 'ends at i in the negated plane'), avoiding a second mirrored implementation. Baseline is a memoized O(n^2) DP directly over coordinates[][], no repo primitive.
problems.notes: Two strategies: MaxPathLengthByBruteForce (memoized O(n^2) DP) and MaxPathLengthBySegmentTree (O(n log n) coordinate-compressed sweep). Verified against LeetCode's 2 published examples by hand and via the Theory tests (4/4 passing), plus a 500-trial randomized cross-check between both strategies (temporary scratch test, removed before finishing) with n up to 30 and coordinates up to 20x20 - all agreed. All four projects (DSAExperimentation, .LeetCode, .Tests, .Benchmarks) build clean in Release.

problems.title: Minimum Number of Valid Strings to Form Target I
problems.primitivesUsed: Algorithms.StringMatching.ZFunction.Compute over word + sentinel + target (per word), reused unmodified, gives the longest-common-prefix-with-target array in one O(word.Length+target.Length) pass; folding the max of that array over every word yields reach[i] = longest valid string startable at i. reach[] then feeds a plain O(n) Jump-Game-II greedy sweep (no repo container needed - just int arrays), shared by both strategies.
problems.notes: Fetched the real problem statement via WebSearch/raw GitHub (LeetCode itself returns 403 to WebFetch) since it differs from the commonly-misremembered single-word version: words is an array, a string is valid if it's a prefix of ANY word in words. Two strategies: MinValidStringsByBruteForce (O(target.Length * sum(words[i].Length)) char-by-char scan) and MinValidStringsByZFunctionAcrossWords (composed). Verified against all 3 published examples (including the -1 unreachable case) via Theory tests (6/6 passing), plus a 500-trial randomized cross-check against the brute force (temporary scratch test, removed before finishing) over a 2-letter alphabet - all agreed. All four projects build clean in Release.

problems.title: Minimum Number of Valid Strings to Form Target II
problems.primitivesUsed: Same composition as Part I (Algorithms.StringMatching.ZFunction.Compute per word, folded into reach[], fed to a Jump-Game-II greedy sweep) - self-contained per ARCHITECTURE.md 17.3 rather than referencing the Part I solution class, mirroring the existing MinimumTimeToRevertWordToInitialStateI/II precedent exactly. words.length<=100 keeps the O(numWords*target.Length + sum(words[i].Length)) composed strategy fast at Part II's 10x-larger (5*10^4) bound, where the brute-force baseline is no longer practical at full scale (benchmarked only at a fraction of it, same convention as MinimumTimeToRevertWordToInitialStateII).
problems.notes: Same 3 published examples as Part I (confirmed identical via the fetched problem statements). Two strategies, Theory tests 6/6 passing; correctness already cross-verified via Part I's 500-trial randomized fuzz test since the algorithm is identical. All four projects build clean in Release.

problems.title: Find the Occurrence of First Almost Equal Substring
problems.primitivesUsed: DSAExperimentation.Algorithms.StringMatching.ZFunction.Compute (existing primitive, reused not extended) - two self-referential Z-function passes, one over pattern+sentinel+s and one over the reverse of both, give forward/backward match-run lengths at every position in O(n+m); a window qualifies iff forward[start]+backward[windowEnd] >= windowLength-1 (at most one mismatch). Sentinel '\0' is chosen by this LeetCode-tier caller, not by ZFunction itself, since only the caller can assume the problem's lowercase-only alphabet excludes it (mirrors ZFunction's own doc comment on why it can't make that assumption generically). Baseline arm IndexOfFirstAlmostEqualSubstringByBruteForce is a first-class O(n*m) direct-count method under the same test theory.
problems.notes: Verified against all 4 published LeetCode examples (incl. the -1 no-match case and the single-character pattern edge case) for both strategies; DSAExperimentation, DSAExperimentation.LeetCode, DSAExperimentation.Tests and DSAExperimentation.Benchmarks all build clean; Tests/Architecture/LayeringTests passes. Benchmark workload (s all 'a', pattern all 'a' except a trailing "bb") forces both arms through a full, match-free scan - confirmed via a throwaway smoke test (written, run, then deleted) that both strategies return -1 and agree at the exact benchmark input shape (Length 200 and 5000).

problems.title: Find the K-th Character in String Game I
problems.primitivesUsed: System.Numerics.BitOperations.PopCount (same BCL primitive already used elsewhere in this LeetCode tier, e.g. MaximumStrongPairXORII/I) for the closed-form KthCharacterByBitCount arm - popcount(k-1) mod 26 is the total cyclic shift applied to the seed 'a'. No repo DataStructures/Algorithms primitive needed beyond that; KthCharacterBySimulation is the plain textbook baseline (a List<char>, doubling and shifting each round).
problems.notes: Verified against both published LeetCode examples (k=5 -> 'b', k=10 -> 'c') for both strategies, cross-checked by hand-tracing the simulation. DSAExperimentation.LeetCode/.Tests/.Benchmarks all build clean; Tests/Architecture/LayeringTests passes.

problems.title: Find the K-th Character in String Game II
problems.primitivesUsed: No DataStructures/Algorithms primitive composition was needed or attempted - both arms are plain arithmetic/simulation (a List<char> doubling walk for the baseline; a backward trace over a k-capped long[] length array for the optimal arm, since k can reach 10^16). Nothing in DataStructures/Algorithms models 'position under repeated doubling with per-round marking', so there was nothing existing to reuse here beyond the same doubling/shift rule Game I (#3304) already encodes independently in its own solution file.
problems.notes: Verified against both published LeetCode examples (k=5, ops=[0,0,0] -> 'a'; k=10, ops=[0,1,0,1] -> 'b') for both strategies, cross-checked by hand-tracing the backward-trace algorithm position-by-position against a manual string build. DSAExperimentation.LeetCode/.Tests/.Benchmarks all build clean; Tests/Architecture/LayeringTests passes. Benchmark workload (alternating 0/1 operations so length always doubles, k pinned to the final length 2^OperationCount) was checked via a throwaway smoke test (written, run, then deleted) confirming both strategies agree and neither throws, at OperationCount 8 and 16 - the brute-force arm stays tractable at that size while still exercising a real word-doubling walk.

problems.title: Sorted GCD Pair Queries
problems.primitivesUsed: Algorithms.Searching.BinarySearch.LowerBound over DataStructures.Sequence.ArraySequence<long>; a problem-local GcdPairCountIndex witness (DSAExperimentation.LeetCode/SortedGcdPairQueries/GcdPairCountIndex.cs) doing divisor-sieve exact-gcd pair counting, the same tier-4 'witness that answers one problem' shape as CountWaysToBuildRoomsInAnAntColony's RoomWaysAlgebra
problems.notes: AnswerQueriesByBruteForce (private Euclidean Gcd + Array.Sort, matching this repo's existing NumberOfDifferentSubsequencesGCDs inline-Gcd convention) vs AnswerQueriesByGcdCountingSieve (hoisted GcdPairCountIndex overload for [GlobalSetup]). Verified against all 3 published LeetCode examples plus a random 300-element/200-query workload where both strategies agree.

problems.title: Find the Number of Possible Ways for an Event
problems.primitivesUsed: Algorithms.DynamicProgramming.Memoizer (TState=performer count, TResult=the whole DP row f(i,0..x)) + Domain.Modular.ModularArithmetic (Modulo, Power)
problems.notes: NumberOfWaysByBruteForceEnumeration (literal x^n stage-assignment enumeration + distinct-stage tally) vs NumberOfWaysByStagePartitionMemo (single Memoizer.Memoize call building the O(n*x) DP table, ModularArithmetic.Power folding in y^stages). Verified against all 3 published examples (n=1,x=2,y=3->6; n=5,x=2,y=1->32; n=3,x=3,y=4->684) plus brute-force-vs-memo agreement over n=1..10, x=1..4, y=1..4.

problems.title: Find the Sequence of Strings Appeared on the Screen
problems.primitivesUsed: DataStructures.DynamicArray.DynamicArray<char> reused unmodified as the on-screen growable buffer, the same cross-domain reuse DataStructures.Sequence.DynamicArraySequence already establishes
problems.notes: StringSequenceByStringBuilder (BCL StringBuilder baseline) vs StringSequenceByGrowableBuffer (this repo's DynamicArray<char>, Add for a key-1 press, Set(Count-1,...) for a key-2 roll). Verified against both published examples plus an all-'z' 400-char worst case and a random 200-char target, both strategies agreeing exactly.

problems.title: Check if DFS Strings Are Palindromes
problems.primitivesUsed: DataStructures.Graph.Engines.Dags.Trees.ParentArrayTree/RootedTreeNode (reused unmodified for the parent-array tree, same as CountWaysToBuildRoomsInAnAntColony) and DataStructures.RollingHash.RollingHash (reused unmodified: one global post-order tour builds dfs(0) once, then a forward RollingHash and a RollingHash over the reversed tour answer every node's [start,end) palindrome query in O(1)). No Domain/ addition.
problems.notes: IsPalindromeByBruteForce (rebuilds dfs(i) per node, O(n^2)) vs IsPalindromeByEulerTourRollingHash (single O(n) tour + O(1) RollingHash comparisons per node). Verified by hand-tracing 3 examples (a 6-node two-level tree, a 5-node star, and a 1-node tree); all 6 test cases pass.

problems.title: Find the Number of Subsequences With Equal GCD
problems.primitivesUsed: Algorithms.DynamicProgramming.Memoizer (reused unmodified for the (index, gcd1, gcd2) memoized recurrence, same composition CountTheNumberOfSquareFreeSubsets uses) and Domain.Modular.ModularArithmetic.Modulo (reused unmodified for the 1e9+7 reporting convention). A tiny private Gcd helper mirrors the one already inline in SortedGcdPairQueriesSolution rather than adding a new primitive.

problems.title: Make Array Elements Equal to Zero
problems.primitivesUsed: No repo primitive needed - pure array/arithmetic composition (like TwoSum's brute force). CountValidSelectionsByBruteForceSimulation directly simulates LeetCode's bounce-and-decrement walk on a scratch array copy; CountValidSelectionsByPrefixSumBalance is an O(n) left/right prefix-sum balance check. problems.title: Digit Operations to Make Two Integers Equal
problems.primitivesUsed: Algorithms/ShortestPaths/ShortestPath.Dijkstra (existing repo primitive, edge weight = target node's value, matching LC 3377's 'cost = sum of every value n takes' rule; final answer adds n itself back in since Dijkstra's source distance starts at Zero). A new problem-local IEdgeTopology witness was added (DigitStepNode/DigitStepTopology/DigitStepGraph, all in the LeetCode/DigitOperationsToMakeTwoIntegersEqual folder per ARCHITECTURE.md 17.3's 'a witness answering one problem lives in that problem's folder, not Domain/'), mirroring the existing FindEdgesInShortestPaths/EdgeGraphNode+EdgeGraphTopology+EdgeGraph pattern exactly. No new DataStructures/ or Algorithms/ primitive was created. MinOperationsByBruteForceDijkstra is a BCL PriorityQueue+Dictionary baseline that reuses DigitStepGraph's DigitMutations/IsPrime helpers for the problem's own digit-move and primality rules (same split OpenTheLockSolution's MinTurnsByMutationQueue makes with LockGraph). Verified against all three LeetCode examples (10,12->85; 4,8->-1; 6,2->-1).

problems.title: Count Connected Components in LCM Graph
problems.primitivesUsed: DataStructures/DisjointSet (DisjointSet, dense-int-indexed forest) - used as an index-space forest for the pairwise-lcm baseline and as a value-space forest sized threshold+1 for the composed multiple-union strategy. No Domain/ type needed; gcd/lcm computed by a private helper, matching this repo's other unmigrated gcd baselines.
problems.notes: Verified against LeetCode's 2 published examples plus a 3000-trial randomized fuzz cross-check of both strategies against each other (0 mismatches).

problems.title: Transformed Array
problems.primitivesUsed: None - pure circular-index arithmetic over the input array; no DataStructures/Algorithms/Domain primitive applies. Baseline is a literal one-step-at-a-time walk, composed strategy is the one-shot modulo formula.
problems.notes: Verified against both of LeetCode's published examples.

problems.title: Maximum Area Rectangle With Point Constraints I
problems.primitivesUsed: DataStructures/Set (Set<(int,int)>) for O(1) opposite-corner existence checks in the composed diagonal-scan strategy; baseline is a quadruple-combination scan. Set<T> also gives the hoisted (points, corners) overload used by [GlobalSetup].
problems.notes: Found and fixed a real bug while verifying: the corner-lookup strategy originally normalized to (minX,maxY)/(maxX,minY) before checking corner existence, which is wrong when the sampled diagonal pair is itself the anti-diagonal (it degenerates into re-confirming the pair's own two points). Fixed to check (x1,y2)/(x2,y1) on raw coordinates, which are always the true opposite corners. Verified against all 3 published examples plus a 3000-trial fuzz cross-check against the brute-force baseline (0 mismatches post-fix). Only Part I (small n) is in scope here; Part II (#3382) is a separate, harder problem not requested.

problems.title: Maximum Area Rectangle With Point Constraints II
problems.primitivesUsed: DataStructures/SegmentTree (SegmentTree<int, MaxOperation<int>>) as a point-update/range-max index over compressed y, composed with a hand-written left-to-right x-column sweep and a Dictionary-based open-edge tracker for the O(n log n) composed strategy (MaxAreaBySweepSegmentTree); baseline (MaxAreaByQuadrupleScan) is a self-contained O(n^5) brute force, independent of Part I's class. This is the 'genuinely different approach' Part I's own doc comment flagged as needed for Part II's n <= 2e5 constraint.
problems.notes: LeetCode's real signature for Part II is (int[] xCoord, int[] yCoord), not int[][] points like Part I. Verified against all 3 published examples (from doocs/leetcode mirror, since leetcode.com itself 403s WebFetch) plus a 20,000-trial fuzz cross-check of the sweep strategy against the quadruple-scan baseline (0 mismatches) before deleting the scratch fuzz test. The fuzz run caught a real bug in my first derivation: the open-edge tracker must advance its recorded xLeft to the current column on EVERY re-occurrence of a (y1,y2) edge, not only when the segment-tree query detects blocking - because the re-occurrence's own two points sit exactly on that edge's y1/y2 border at an intermediate column, which always invalidates any wider rectangle crossing over it regardless of what the tree query reports.

problems.title: Subsequences with a Unique Middle Mode I
problems.primitivesUsed: Domain/Modular/ModularArithmetic for the 1e9+7 modulus. No other repo primitive fits (this is pure combinatorial counting over running Dictionary<int,int> frequency tables, not a topology/graph/search problem), so the O(n^2) composed strategy (CountMiddleModeSubsequencesByModularCombinatorics) is hand-derived closed-form combinatorics, matching how Part I's own corner-lookup strategy is hand-rolled geometry over just Set<T>.
problems.notes: Verified against all 3 published examples (doocs/leetcode mirror) plus a 40,000-trial fuzz cross-check of the combinatorial strategy against the O(n^5) brute-force baseline (0 mismatches) before deleting the scratch fuzz test. The fuzz run caught a real bug in my first derivation: the k=0 case (middle value x appears only once among the 5) can NEVER be a valid unique-middle-mode subsequence - with only 4 other elements always present, one of them always ties x's frequency of 1 - so it must contribute 0 unconditionally, not the distinct-pair count I originally computed for it (which incorrectly credited the all-distinct-values case). Fixing that also let two derived quantities (a full 2x2 cross-collision inclusion-exclusion term) drop out as dead code entirely, simplifying the final solution.

problems.title: Count the Number of Arrays with K Matching Adjacent Elements
problems.primitivesUsed: Domain/Modular/ModularArithmetic (Power for modular exponentiation, Inverse for the factorial table) - the same factorial/inverse-factorial-table shape CountAnagramsByModularFactorial and RoomWaysPrecomputedFactorialAlgebra already use for other counting problems, here computing one binomial coefficient C(n-1,k) and one modular power (m-1)^(n-1-k).
problems.notes: Closed-form answer = C(n-1,k) * m * (m-1)^(n-1-k) mod 1e9+7, verified directly against all 3 published examples (doocs/leetcode mirror). Straightforward enough (formula checks out algebraically and matches all examples exactly) that no additional fuzz cross-check was needed beyond the baseline O(m^n) brute-force enumeration matching on the same examples.

problems.title: Substring Matching Pattern
problems.primitivesUsed: Algorithms.StringMatching.PrefixFunctionSearch (KMP FindAll) - no new primitives. Pattern's single '*' splits into prefix/suffix; match exists iff latest suffix occurrence start >= earliest prefix occurrence start + prefix length.
problems.notes: Baseline is an O(n^2)/O(n^3) all-substrings brute force using plain BCL span comparisons. Both strategies pass all 3 LeetCode-published examples. Build clean across all 4 projects; benchmark smoke-run (Dry job) executes without error.

problems.title: Design Task Manager
problems.primitivesUsed: DataStructures.Heap.Heap<Element,MaxHeapOrder<Element>> + DataStructures.HashMap.HashMap<TKey,TValue> - no new primitives. Stateful Design problem, so 'every strategy' is two classes (TaskManagerByLinearScan baseline, TaskManagerByLazyDeletionHeap) sharing an ITaskManagerStrategy surface, plus a problem-local TaskEntry IComparable witness for heap ordering (Priority then TaskId tie-break).
problems.notes: Lazy-deletion heap: fresh TaskEntry pushed on Add/Edit, stale popped entries discarded via a HashMap current-state check on ExecTop (Heap has no decrease-key/remove). Corrected LeetCode's remove-method name to 'rmv' (not 'rm') by fetching the live question via leetcode.com's GraphQL API - no cached LeetCodeCatalog fixture existed for this slug. Both strategies pass the one published call-sequence example. Benchmark smoke-run (Dry job) shows the expected asymptotic gap: at 2000 tasks, linear-scan ~77.6ms vs lazy-deletion-heap ~7.6ms.

problems.title: Maximize Subarray Sum After Removing All Occurrences of One Element
problems.notes: Missing primitive: an augmented 'maximum subarray sum' merge (sum, prefix-max, suffix-max, best) - the classic segment-tree Kadane monoid - as a DataStructures.SegmentTree.ICombineOperation<Element> witness (or equivalent DSU union-merge). Only scalar Sum/Min/Max/Xor operations exist across SegmentTree/LazySegmentTree/FenwickTree/RangeFenwickTree; grepped Algorithms/ and DataStructures/ for Kadane/MaxSubarray with no matches. Checked and rejected a prefix-sum + range-min-query workaround (Kadane's reset step is non-linear, so it reduces to the same missing monoid). This witness is genuinely general-purpose (no problem-specific content, structurally a peer of Sum/Min/MaxOperation), so it does not qualify for the LeetCode-folder witness exception the way LC1916's RoomWaysAlgebra does. A brute force composing only existing primitives (rerun Kadane per distinct value, O(n*d)) is possible but is a genuinely different, asymptotically worse algorithm than what the problem calls for, so marked blocked per instruction rather than shipped as a misrepresentation of 'solved by composing existing primitives'.

problems.title: Zigzag Grid Traversal With Skip
problems.primitivesUsed: No existing Domain/ or graph-topology type fits (it's pure raster-order iteration, not adjacency - DataStructures.Graph.Grids.Grid/GridTopology model 4-directional passability, an unrelated shape, so nothing was forced there). Baseline (TraverseByIndexFormula) is a plain index-formula scan, no repo type. Composed (TraverseByRowStack) reuses DataStructures.Stack.Stack<int> to undo each right-to-left row by push-then-pop, the same idiom AddBinarySolution.AddByBitStack already uses for LC 67. No new Domain/ or production primitives added.
problems.notes: Verified via a real dotnet build + dotnet test pass. Note for the orchestrator: DSAExperimentation.Tests currently fails to build as a whole because of an unrelated, untracked, in-progress file from a concurrent session (LeetCodeCoverage/DesignTaskManager/DesignTaskManagerTests.cs, error CS0051) - not touched, per the git-safety instructions. problems.title: Minimize the Maximum Edge Weight of Graph
problems.primitivesUsed: `threshold` turns out to be a red herring (any threshold >= 1, the problem's own floor, already suffices, since a reachability tree toward node 0 needs only one outgoing edge per node), so both strategies binary-search the max edge weight and differ only in how feasibility is checked. Added a single-problem witness in the LeetCode/ folder itself (EdgeWeightGraph/EdgeWeightNode/EdgeWeightChildren/EdgeWeightTopology, ARCHITECTURE.md section 17.3), mirroring DataStructures.Graph.Grids.Grid/GridNode/GridChildren/GridTopology's runtime-filtered-adjacency shape. Composed strategy reuses Algorithms.Reducing.Reduce.Graph + DistanceMapReduceAlgebra + BreadthFirstReduceOrder over that topology, the same composition Algorithms.ShortestPaths.Grids.GridShortestPath uses. Baseline is a plain BCL Queue<int>/bool[] BFS over the same EdgeWeightGraph (shared as the hoisted prepared-input overload for both arms). No Domain/ types existed for this or were added; no new DataStructures/Algorithms primitives added.

problems.title: Count Non-Decreasing Subarrays After K Operations
problems.primitivesUsed: Composed strategy (CountByMonotonicDequeWindow) reuses DataStructures.Deque.Deque<(long Value, long Count)> as a run-length-compressed monotonic window over the subarray's prefix-max cost profile - it needs both ends (grow by prepending at the front as the window walks right-to-left, shrink by popping the back), which is why this is genuinely a Deque problem rather than a single-ended Stack<T> one. Baseline (CountByPrefixMaxBruteForce) is plain O(n^2) BCL with an early break. The cost-profile bookkeeping itself is problem-specific content (this problem's own increment-only-repair cost formula), not a generic Algorithms/ operation, so it lives in the solution class rather than as a new primitive. No Domain/ types applied or added.
problems.notes: Hand-derivation of the O(n) sliding-window algorithm initially had a real bug (grew/shrunk the window from the wrong ends, which loses information needed to correctly un-merge a plateau) that a first implementation attempt surfaced as an IndexOutOfRangeException against both LeetCode examples. Re-derived against a known-correct reference algorithm, fixed, and re-verified by hand-tracing both examples field-by-field before re-running the isolated test build, which now passes.

problems.title: Manhattan Distances of All Arrangements of Pieces
problems.primitivesUsed: Domain.Modular.ModularArithmetic (Power/Inverse, existing) for the modular inverse in the closed-form pairwise-distance formula and in the local factorial-based binomial coefficient helper. No new production primitives added. SumByBruteForceArrangements (naive: enumerate every k-cell arrangement and every pair inside it) vs SumByPairwiseDistanceFormula (closed form: sum over cell pairs weighted by C(mn-2,k-2), row/column distance sums via length*(length^2-1)/6). Both verified against both LeetCode published examples (8 and 20).
problems.notes: Not previously covered under any name. Constraints (m,n<=1e5, mn<=1e5) keep the O(mn) factorial precompute in the composed strategy proportional to the problem size.

problems.title: Maximum and Minimum Sums of at Most Size K Subsequences
problems.primitivesUsed: Domain.Modular.ModularArithmetic (Inverse, existing) for the reverse-fill inverse-factorial table in the composed strategy (same trick as CountWaysToBuildRoomsInAnAntColony's RoomWaysPrecomputedFactorialAlgebra, generalized locally rather than duplicated). No new production primitives added. SumByPascalTriangle (BCL-only capped Pascal's-triangle row sums, the baseline) vs SumByFactorialCombinatorics (precomputed factorial/inverse-factorial nCr lookups, the composed strategy). LC caps k<=min(70,n), so both are O(n*k); they differ in technique, not asymptotics - same shape as OpenTheLock's two same-complexity BFS strategies. Verified against all three LeetCode published examples (24, 22, 12 - including the all-duplicates case).
problems.notes: Not previously covered under any name.

problems.title: Maximum and Minimum Sums of at Most Size K Subarrays
problems.primitivesUsed: DataStructures.Stack<Element> (existing repo primitive, aliased as RepoIntStack per this codebase's established Stack<T>/BCL-collision convention) for both monotonic-stack passes (previous strictly-dominant / next non-strictly-dominant index) in the composed strategy. No new production primitives added. SumByBruteForceWindow (O(n*k) incremental sliding window, BCL-only baseline) vs SumByMonotonicStackContribution (O(n) dominance-range + closed-form arithmetic counting of length-<=k subarrays per element, composed strategy). Tie-break convention (strict left / non-strict right) matches this repo's existing unmigrated SumOfSubarrayMinimums precedent for LC 907. Verified against both LeetCode published examples (20, and -6 with a duplicate value and negatives). No modulo in this variant, unlike its subsequence sibling LC 3428 - confirmed via the published examples and constraint magnitudes fitting Int64 outright.
problems.notes: Not previously covered under any name.

problems.title: Frequencies of Shortest Supersequences
problems.primitivesUsed: Algorithms/TopologicalSort/TopologicalSort.TrySort (Kahn's algorithm, reused as an acyclicity check via its documented false-on-cycle return) over a fresh per-candidate induced subgraph built from DataStructures/Graph/Contracts/Ordering's IGraphTopology<T,TChildren>, ListChildren<T> and NaturalChildOrder<T,TChildren>. Two problem-local witness types added in the LeetCode folder (LetterNode/LetterTopology, mirroring Domain/Locks/LockNode+LockTopology) plus a plain parsed-input type LetterGraph - all single-problem per §17.3, no other problem models a letter-precedence graph.
problems.notes: Problem reduces to enumerating every minimum-size feedback-vertex-set of the letter-precedence graph (doubled letters break every cycle; frequency 2 for doubled, 1 otherwise). Baseline arm (SupersequenceFrequenciesByDfsSkipSet) is the textbook three-color DFS over BCL adjacency lists, matching the known reference algorithm exactly; composed arm (SupersequenceFrequenciesByTopologicalSort) answers the same 'is this subset's induced subgraph acyclic' question via TopologicalSort.TrySort. Verified against all 3 published LC examples (order-independent comparison, since output order is unspecified) plus a 200-word benchmark-scale smoke run. All 4 projects build clean; Tests/Architecture/LayeringTests passes.

problems.title: Minimum Increments for Target Multiples in an Array
problems.primitivesUsed: Algorithms/DynamicProgramming/Memoizer, reused as-is for the composed arm's top-down bitmask DP (state = (Index, CoveredMask)), matching its documented Y-combinator recursion shape exactly. Baseline arm is the same recurrence written as a plain bottom-up long[] array DP (no repo primitive, by design). A problem-local TargetLcmTable record (not a repo primitive) precomputes per-subset LCMs as the hoisted-overload's prepared input.
problems.notes: target.Length <= 4 (LC constraint) keeps the bitmask small (<=16 states). Verified both arms agree and match all 3 published LC examples by hand-trace and by test, plus a 1000-element benchmark-scale smoke run confirming baseline/composed agreement. Benchmark [Params] capped at 1,000 nums (not LC's 5*10^4 ceiling) because the memoized arm recurses one real stack frame per nums element and Memoizer is documented as real-recursion-only - this stays within a safe stack depth rather than chasing LC's own input ceiling. All 4 projects build clean; layering tests pass.

problems.title: Separate Squares II
problems.primitivesUsed: DataStructures/IntervalSet/IntervalSet<long>, reused directly as the per-band covered-x-length accumulator in a y-coordinate sweep (its merged, non-overlapping closed-interval invariant IS the union length needed). Baseline arm hand-sorts/merges the same per-band intervals via a plain BCL List, deliberately not IntervalSet. A problem-local Square record (not a repo primitive) is the hoisted-overload's prepared input type.
problems.notes: Sweep walks square Y/Y+L boundaries as band edges; band area = (IntervalSet-merged x-coverage) * (band height); split line found via cumulative-area interpolation. One correctness fix versus my first draft: LC asks for the *minimum* splitting y, so the search now returns as soon as cumulative area reaches half exactly at a band boundary rather than drifting into a later, equally-valid but larger, zero-width band. Verified against both published LC examples (Assert precision=5, matching LC's 1e-5 tolerance) plus a 200-square benchmark-scale smoke run confirming baseline/composed agreement. All 4 projects build clean; layering tests pass.

problems.title: Shortest Matching Substring
problems.primitivesUsed: Algorithms.StringMatching.PrefixFunctionSearch (KMP FindAll) for ascending occurrence lists of each literal part of p1*p2*p3; Algorithms.Searching.BinarySearch.LowerBound over DataStructures.Sequence.ArraySequence<int> to find the earliest occurrence at/after a floor. Added two problem-local witnesses (folder-scoped per ARCHITECTURE.md 17.3, not Domain/): MatchPattern (splits p on '*') and PatternOccurrences (hoisted-overload input bundling the three KMP occurrence lists, mirroring OpenTheLockSolution's LockGraph hoist). Baseline strategy ShortestLengthByBruteForceIndexOf uses plain BCL string.IndexOf. No new production primitives invented.
problems.notes: Verified against all 4 published LeetCode examples (incl. the two-empty-star and no-match cases) via `dotnet test`; benchmark dry-run smoke-tested successfully.

problems.title: Length of Longest V-Shaped Diagonal Segment
problems.primitivesUsed: None from DataStructures/Algorithms fit: DataStructures.Graph.Grids.GridTopology/GridChildren only model orthogonal 4-neighbor BFS adjacency, not a directed diagonal walk with a per-position value obligation (1,2,0,2,0,...) and a one-shot clockwise turn. Both strategies (naive turn-at-every-position walk, and an O(rows*cols*4) directional-DP with two int[,,] tables) are plain array composition over the raw int[][] grid, matching how OpenTheLockSolution's own naive baseline is deliberately primitive-free. Considered Algorithms.DynamicProgramming.Memoizer, but its per-call cache is scoped to a single top-level query (see Memoizer.cs doc comment); querying it once per (row,col,direction) - as this table needs - would rebuild overlapping predecessor chains from scratch on every call (worst-case O(n^3) instead of O(n^2)), so plain iterative table-fill was used instead of forcing an awkward fit.
problems.notes: Corrected the value sequence via a web check of the official examples mid-task: the alternation is 1 then 2,0,2,0,... (not 1,2,1,2 as first assumed from the task's own paraphrase). All 4 published examples (grid arrays fetched from the LeetCode-mirrored README, incl. the one-turn, straight-diagonal and single-cell cases) pass for both strategies via `dotnet test`; benchmark dry-run smoke-tested successfully.

problems.title: Check If Digits Are Equal in String After Operations I
problems.primitivesUsed: None - s.Length <= 10 (LC's own Part I bound) is too small for any repo DataStructures/Algorithms primitive to earn its place; Domain.Modular.ModularArithmetic is pinned to mod 1e9+7 by its own doc comment and doesn't apply to this problem's mod 10. Both strategies are plain digit-array composition: direct repeated adjacent-sum reduction, and reading the two final digits off row (n-2) of Pascal's triangle (built in-place, no repo primitive) since that row's binomial coefficients are exactly what n-2 reduction steps compute.
problems.notes: Verified against both published LeetCode examples (3902->true, 34789->false) via `dotnet test`; also hand-verified the Pascal-row closed form arithmetically against both examples. Benchmark dry-run smoke-tested successfully.

problems.title: Check If Digits Are Equal in String After Operations II
problems.primitivesUsed: None from DataStructures/Algorithms (same as the already-migrated Part I). The combinatorics (Lucas' theorem mod 2 and mod 5 plus CRT, to read C(n-2,j) mod 10 without materializing a Pascal row) are problem-local, written directly in the solution class. Domain.Modular.ModularArithmetic was considered but is hardcoded to mod 1e9+7 via Fermat's little theorem, not reusable here.
problems.notes: Two strategies: AreEqualByAdjacentSumReduction (baseline, O(n^2) direct simulation) and AreEqualByLucasBinomialCoefficients (composed, O(n log n)). Verified against both LeetCode examples plus a scratch cross-check (200 random strings up to length 300, both strategies agreeing) that was removed before finishing. Benchmark confirms the story: at length 5000 baseline takes ~15.6ms vs ~1.2ms for the Lucas strategy.
problems.strategies: AreEqualByAdjacentSumReduction (baseline: perform the stated reduction directly, O(n^2), the arm Lucas has to beat at n approaching 1e5); AreEqualByLucasBinomialCoefficients (BinomialModTwo via Kummer's theorem's bitwise submask check, BinomialModFive via Lucas' theorem over a precomputed 5x5 Pascal table, combined per coefficient by CRT)

problems.title: Maximize the Distance Between Points on a Square
problems.primitivesUsed: DSAExperimentation.Algorithms.Searching.BinarySearch.LowerBound composed over DSAExperimentation.DataStructures.Sequence.ArraySequence<long> (sorted perimeter offsets) for the 'next point at least gap away' step inside a binary-search-on-the-answer.
problems.notes: Two strategies: MaxDistanceByLinearScan (baseline, linear inner scan) and MaxDistanceBySortedGreedy (composed, BinarySearch.LowerBound inner hop). Both have a hoisted ArraySequence<long> overload (via public ToSortedPerimeterPositions) so benchmarks charge mapping+sorting to GlobalSetup. Verified against all three LeetCode examples plus a scratch cross-check (300 random configurations, both strategies agreeing with each other and with an O(2^n) brute-force over real Manhattan distance) removed before finishing.
problems.strategies: MaxDistanceByLinearScan (baseline: binary search on the answer, but the inner 'next point >= gap away' step is a plain forward scan); MaxDistanceBySortedGreedy (composed: same binary search, but that inner step is BinarySearch.LowerBound over the sorted ArraySequence<long> of offsets). Both have a LeetCode-shaped overload (int side, int[][] points, int k) and a hoisted overload taking the pre-sorted ArraySequence<long> via the solution's own public ToSortedPerimeterPositions, so a benchmark charges the mapping+sort to [GlobalSetup].

problems.title: Permutations IV
problems.primitivesUsed: DSAExperimentation.DataStructures.FenwickTree.FenwickTree<int,SumOperation<int>> (one presence tree per parity pool) + DSAExperimentation.Algorithms.Searching.BinarySearch.LowerBound (over a local IRandomAccessSequence<int> witness wrapping the tree's PrefixQuery) for O(log^2 n) order-statistics 'find and remove the r-th still-unused value'.
problems.notes: 'Alternating' here means adjacent elements differ in parity (verified against all 3 examples), so completions-from-any-valid-prefix = remainingOdds! * remainingEvens!, independent of which values were placed - ordinary factorial-number-system unranking, no Entringer-number DP needed. Two strategies: KthPermutationByBigIntegerRank (baseline: BCL List<int> + exact BigInteger factorials) and KthPermutationByFenwickOrderStatistics (composed: FenwickTree + BinarySearch.LowerBound + saturating-long factorials capped at 2e15). Verified beyond the 3 published examples via two scratch cross-checks (exhaustive brute-force enumeration for n=1..8 over every valid/invalid k; agreement at n in {20,50,100} with k up to ~1e15) removed before finishing.
problems.strategies: KthPermutationByBigIntegerRank (baseline: BCL List<int> pools with List<T>.RemoveAt/Remove plus exact BigInteger factorials, no repo primitives); KthPermutationByFenwickOrderStatistics (composed: FenwickTree presence pools plus BinarySearch.LowerBound for r-th-unused lookup, with saturating long factorials capped at 2e15 standing in for BigInteger)

problems.title: Lexicographically Smallest Generated String
problems.primitivesUsed: Algorithms/StringMatching/ZFunction.Compute (str2's self-overlap array validates overlapping 'T' windows in O(1) and bounds the fill pass to O(n+m)) for the second strategy; the baseline strategy uses only plain char arrays. No Domain/ type needed - this problem fixes no reusable modulus/vertex-set/graph shape.
problems.notes: Two strategies: GenerateStringByDirectFill (O(n*m) textbook: overwrite+compare per 'T', per-character F-window comparison) and GenerateStringByZFunctionConsistency (ZFunction-backed consistency check + suffix-only writes). Verified against LeetCode's 3 published examples plus 3 hand-derived cases covering every branch the published examples miss: a consistent overlapping-T merge ('TT'/'aa'->'aaa'), an F-window needing its rightmost free char bumped ('TF'/'a'->'ab'), and an F-window fully pinned by surrounding T's with no room to bump, proven genuinely unsatisfiable by hand ('TFTF'/'aaa'->'').

problems.title: Fruits Into Baskets II
problems.primitivesUsed: None - n <= 100 makes the direct O(n^2) leftmost-fit rescan this problem's own intended solution; no repo primitive earns its keep at this size.
problems.notes: Single strategy CountUnplacedByBruteForce, matching the ValidParentheses/MergeTwoSortedLists precedent for single-strategy problems in this repo.

problems.title: Fruits Into Baskets III
problems.primitivesUsed: DataStructures/SegmentTree/SegmentTree<int, MaxOperation<int>> (used baskets deactivated via MaxOperation<int>.Identity, the same move BlockPlacementQueriesSolution already makes on its own gap tree) plus DataStructures/AlgorithmConstants.HalvingFactor for the binary-search midpoint.
problems.notes: Same rule as LC 3477 at n <= 1e5. Baseline CountUnplacedByBruteForce (O(n^2), identical shape to II) plus CountUnplacedBySegmentTreeSearch: 'leftmost basket >= quantity' via a private LeftmostBasketAtLeast binary search over the segment tree's public Query (Query(low,mid) >= target is monotonic in mid), O(log^2 n) per fruit since SegmentTree exposes no direct tree descent - an honest cost of composing through its existing public surface rather than reimplementing traversal.

problems.title: Maximize Subarrays After Removing One Conflicting Pair
problems.primitivesUsed: DataStructures/DynamicArray/DynamicArray<int> as the per-right-endpoint conflict bucket in the composed strategy (MaxSubarraysByGroupedBoundSweep). No new production primitive needed: the O(n+m) algorithm (bucket conflicting pairs by max(a,b), sweep right=1..n tracking the two largest min(a,b) bounds seen so far, accumulate per-bound removal gain) is plain array/counting logic, ported and numerically verified against both published LeetCode examples (n=4 -> 9, n=5 -> 12) by hand-tracing before coding. Baseline MaxSubarraysByBruteForce is true O(n^2*m^2) exhaustive subarray-vs-pair checking, no repo primitives, deliberately naive.

problems.title: Unique 3-Digit Even Numbers
problems.primitivesUsed: Algorithms/Backtracking/Backtrack.Search + DataStructures/Set/Set<int>, composed exactly the way Permutations' PermuteByBacktracking already does (choose/explore/unchoose over index positions via Backtrack.Search, capped at length 3 via IsSolution/Candidates). Baseline CountByIndexPermutationScan is plain recursion over a BCL used[] array + BCL HashSet<int>, no repo primitives, mirroring PermuteBySpecializedRecursion.

problems.title: Design Spreadsheet
problems.primitivesUsed: DataStructures/HashMap/HashMap<string,int> as the cell store in SpreadsheetByHashMap, contrasted against a BCL Dictionary<string,int> baseline (SpreadsheetByDictionary) - same shape as DesignTaskManager's shared ITaskManagerStrategy interface plus two implementing classes, replayed via a small Op-script harness (SpreadsheetOp) mirroring TaskManagerOp.

problems.title: Longest Common Prefix of K Strings After Removal
problems.primitivesUsed: DataStructures/Graph/Engines/Dags/Trees: LowercaseTrie<int>/LowercaseTrieNode<int>/LowercaseTrieTopology<int> (reused as-is). Algorithms/Reducing: Reduce.Tree + DepthFirstReduceOrder + the existing DistanceMapReduceAlgebra (reused as-is, unmodified). One new problem-local IReduceAlgebra witness, SubtreeWordCountAlgebra.cs, added in the LeetCode/ problem folder (ARCHITECTURE.md 17.3's 'witness used by this problem alone' allowance, mirrors RoomWaysAlgebra precedent) for post-order subtree word-count. Also added a benchmark-only fixture DSAExperimentation.Benchmarks/Fixtures/LongestCommonPrefixOfKStringsWorkloads.cs.
problems.notes: Both LeetCode examples verified (incl. duplicate-heavy example 1). Algorithm: deepest globally-qualifying trie depth (precomputed once) applies as-is to any word whose own length is shorter than it; otherwise an O(word length) walk from that depth back to the root checks whether this word's own removal (decrementing its path nodes by exactly its own multiplicity contribution) was the sole thing keeping that depth qualified. O(total input length) overall.

problems.title: Properties Graph
problems.primitivesUsed: DataStructures/DisjointSet/DisjointSet (+ DisjointSetForest, reused as-is) and DataStructures/Set/Set<T> (bulk-seeding constructor, TryAdd, Has). Baseline uses a hand-rolled BCL union-find + HashSet<int> per ARCHITECTURE.md 17.5. Also added a benchmark-only fixture DSAExperimentation.Benchmarks/Fixtures/PropertiesGraphWorkloads.cs.
problems.notes: All three LeetCode examples verified. Noted (non-blocking) gap: Set<T> has no enumerator, so the composed strategy also keeps each row's distinct values as a plain int[] (produced via Set<T>.TryAdd) alongside the Set used for membership testing, since intersect-counting needs to iterate one side's elements.

problems.title: Minimum Cost to Divide Array Into Subarrays
problems.primitivesUsed: Algorithms/DynamicProgramming/Memoizer (reused as-is), same shared-PartitionStep + Dictionary-memo-vs-Memoizer pairing as the already-migrated MinimumSumOfValuesByDividingArraySolution. No Domain/ type needed. Also added a benchmark-only fixture DSAExperimentation.Benchmarks/Fixtures/MinimumCostToDivideArrayIntoSubarraysWorkloads.cs.
problems.notes: Both LeetCode examples verified (hand-derived first, e.g. (3+1+1)*(4+6)=50, then confirmed by the running code). Key move: the k*i (segment-index) term looks like it needs a (position, segment-count) 2D DP state, but a summation-by-parts identity (sum_i i*x_i = sum_t SuffixCostSum(start_t)) makes the k-term additive per segment start position, collapsing state back to plain 1D position - avoiding any need for a convex-hull-trick/Li-Chao-tree primitive this repo doesn't have.

problems.title: Maximize Active Section with Trade II
problems.primitivesUsed: DataStructures.SegmentTree.SegmentTree<int, MaxOperation<int>> (already existed, unmodified) composed with a new problem-local witness ActiveSectionTradeIndex (LeetCode/MaximizeActiveSectionWithTradeII/ActiveSectionTradeIndex.cs, per §17.3 - a witness meaningful only to this problem). No new DataStructures/ or Algorithms/ primitives. Baseline MaxActiveAfterTradeByRunScan is a from-scratch run-length-encode-and-scan per query (pure BCL). Composed MaxActiveAfterTradeByRangeMaxIndex groups s into zero-runs, and range-max-queries the static array of adjacent-zero-run-pair sums via SegmentTree<int,MaxOperation<int>> - the same generic range-max structure other migrated problems (FruitsIntoBasketsIII, MaximumAreaRectangleWithPointConstraintsII) already use, just with a new Element/witness pairing.
problems.notes: Hard problem; the literal 'trade' definition (mandatory sacrifice-then-fill, everything outside [l,r] untouched) required deriving the answer formula from scratch since a first web search summary was subtly misleading (windowed vs whole-string active count). Verified against the raw LeetCode README's Chinese-language step-by-step explanations for all 4 published examples by hand before coding, then proved by construction that the 'pair adjacent zero-runs around any interior one-run, take the max' formula is complete (an independent 'max zero-run minus min interior one-run' term is always dominated, so it's never needed) - cross-checked against a public reference solution's own logic, which uses the same reduction via a sparse table (functionally identical to this repo's SegmentTree<int,MaxOperation<int>> used here, just O(log n) instead of O(1) per query). Both strategies pass all 4 published examples (8/8 test assertions). Benchmark dry-run at n=200/2000 shows the expected shape: RangeMaxIndex runs in ~0.2-0.4x of RunScan's time with zero extra allocation vs growing allocation for the baseline.

problems.title: Minimum Pair Removal to Sort Array I
problems.primitivesUsed: DataStructures.Heap.Heap<Element, MinHeapOrder<Element>> (already existed, unmodified) with a new problem-local IComparable witness PairCandidate (LeetCode/MinimumPairRemovalToSortArrayI/PairCandidate.cs, per §17.3, mirroring DesignTaskManagerSolution's TaskEntry precedent). No new DataStructures/ or Algorithms/ primitives. Baseline MinOperationsByBruteForce is BCL List<int> with a full rescan-for-min-pair and rescan-for-sorted each round. Composed MinOperationsByLazyPairHeap uses the Heap plus plain int[] next/prev/alive arrays and an incrementally-maintained inversion counter (the same lazy-deletion-heap idiom DesignTaskManagerSolution.TaskManagerByLazyDeletionHeap already established, since Heap has no decrease-key/remove).
problems.notes: Hand-traced the lazy-deletion-heap strategy against LC's own example ([5,2,3,1] -> 2 operations) during design and caught a real bug in my first draft (the merged pair's own violation contribution wasn't being subtracted before re-adding its replacement neighbors, double-counting/dropping an inversion) - fixed by having BoundaryViolations subtract all three of the (before,left), (left,right), (right,after) pair contributions the merge invalidates, not just the two boundary ones. Both strategies pass both published examples (4/4). Benchmark stays within the official 'I' constraint (n<=50, unlike its Hard 'II' sibling) per the task's honesty about what regime this variant actually runs in; at that size the heap strategy's constant overhead makes it slower than brute force in a dry-run smoke test, which is expected and consistent with the problem's own small-n cap - the composed strategy's asymptotic advantage (O(1) amortized pair-selection and O(1) sortedness-check vs brute force's O(n) each) would only show at larger n, which 'I' never actually exercises.

problems.title: Implement Router
problems.primitivesUsed: DataStructures.Queue.Queue<Element>, DataStructures.Set.Set<Element>, DataStructures.HashMap.HashMap<TKey,TValue>, DataStructures.DynamicArray.DynamicArray<Element>, DataStructures.Sequence.DynamicArraySequence<Element>, and Algorithms.Searching.BinarySearch.LowerBound/UpperBound - all already existed, unmodified, no new primitives. Design-category problem (stateful instance API), so 'every strategy' is two classes (RouterByLinearScan baseline, RouterByBinarySearchIndex composed) sharing an IRouterStrategy surface, matching DesignTaskManagerSolution's established shape for this problem category. A private nested DestinationLog class (per-destination timestamp log + start index) is the only problem-local plumbing, not a separate witness type.
problems.notes: getCount composes BinarySearch.LowerBound/UpperBound over each destination's own append-only DynamicArray<int> of timestamps (kept sorted for free via LC's own 'calls arrive in non-decreasing timestamp order' guarantee), clipped by a start index that only ever advances - since both addPacket's memory-limit eviction and forwardPacket always remove the same global-FIFO-oldest packet, and that packet is provably also the oldest survivor for its own destination under the monotonic-timestamp guarantee, so no rescan is ever needed. Verified against both published examples (fetched the raw LeetCode README via GitHub mirror since leetcode.com itself returns 403 to automated fetches) - example 2 in particular exercises the 'no packets left to forward' empty-array case. Both strategies pass both examples (4/4 assertions), including the int[]-vs-bool-vs-int mixed-return-type script harness (RouterOp.Apply boxes to object?, with an explicit int[] structural-comparison branch in the test's AssertMatches to avoid relying on boxed-array equality semantics).

problems.title: Minimum Pair Removal to Sort Array II
problems.primitivesUsed: DataStructures/Heap (Heap<Element,TOrder> + MinHeapOrder<Element>) as a lazy-deletion priority queue over adjacent-pair sums; DataStructures/DoublyLinkedList (DoublyLinkedList<T> + DoublyLinkedListNode<T>) as the mutable left-to-right adjacency chain; DataStructures/Set (Set<T>, itself composing HashMap<TKey,TValue>) for O(1) reference-identity liveness tracking of surviving nodes. Baseline MinOperationsByBruteForceScan uses a plain List<long> rescan. Verified against LeetCode's 2 published examples plus 500 randomized cross-checks between both strategies (both agreed on every trial; not committed).

problems.title: Shortest Path in a Weighted Tree
problems.primitivesUsed: DataStructures/Queue (Queue<int>) for the BFS that converts edges[] into a parent array, the same conversion MaximumPointsAfterCollectingCoinsFromAllNodesSolution already established; DataStructures/Graph/Engines/Dags/Trees (RootedTreeNode + ParentArrayTree.Build) to materialize that parent array as a tree; DataStructures/Stack (Stack<RootedTreeNode>) for an iterative (non-recursive, chain-safe) pre-order Euler tour producing contiguous per-subtree [TimeIn,TimeOut] ranges; DataStructures/RangeFenwickTree (RangeFenwickTree<long,ScaledSumOperation<long>>) as the range-add/point-query structure - an edge update becomes one RangeAdd over the child's subtree range, a [2,x] query becomes one point Query(TimeIn[x],TimeIn[x]), exactly the use its own doc comment names. Baseline ShortestPathQueriesByBruteForceBfs uses a plain BCL Queue/Dictionary BFS per query. Verified against all 3 published examples (hand-traced by me and passing) plus 300 randomized cross-checks (both strategies agreed on every trial; not committed).

problems.title: Smallest Palindromic Rearrangement I
problems.primitivesUsed: DataStructures/Stack (Stack<char>) - the same 'LIFO order undoes the reversal' composition AddBinarySolution already established for its own two strategies, applied here to building a palindrome's mirrored right half instead of undoing a least-significant-digit-first carry walk. RearrangeByCharArrayReverse is the char-array-plus-manual-reverse counterpart. Verified against all 3 published examples plus 500 randomized cross-checks, each also independently checked for correct multiset and palindrome-ness against a from-scratch reference computation (all passed; not committed).
